prompts.question: Assess the extent to which advisory bodies of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people can improve economic outcomes when governments retain the final decision.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: Two regional towns each run a program to create jobs for local residents. In Town A, an Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander advisory body has advised on the program's design since it started, and employment rose by 8 per cent over two years. In Town B, the program was designed without an advisory body, and employment rose by 5 per cent over the same period. The towns differ in population size and industry mix, and no evaluation has controlled for these differences.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Assesses the extent of advisory influence with sustained analysis of how advice shapes programs, weighing the limits of the Town A and Town B comparison, and reaches a reasoned judgement
5 marks: Assesses the extent of influence with accurate analysis of at least two mechanisms and a link to the scenario, with some judgement
4 marks: Analyses how advisory bodies affect economic outcomes with some accuracy, linking to the scenario without a clear judgement
3 marks: Describes the role of advisory bodies with some accuracy and a limited link to economic outcomes
2 marks: Identifies a role of advisory bodies with a basic reference to the scenario
1 mark: Makes a general statement about community participation in policy
markerNotes: Reward the distinction between correlation and causation when the Town A and Town B results are interpreted
Credit a judgement on the extent of influence, such as advice mattering most when the government commits to adopt and fund it
commonStudentErrors: Concluding that the advisory body caused the 8 per cent rise in employment without considering other differences between the towns
Treating advice as binding on government, so the body is assumed to control the outcome

sampleAnswers.answer: Advisory bodies can improve economic outcomes mainly by making programs more relevant to the people they serve. Local knowledge of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities can help design employment programs that suit local skills, reduce the risk of programs failing, and build trust, which can increase participation. These mechanisms are real but indirect, because an advisory body only recommends, and government policy is set by the minister. Employment rose 8 per cent in Town A and 5 per cent in Town B, but this is a correlation rather than proof of causation: the towns differ in population size and industry mix, and no evaluation has controlled for these differences. A fair assessment would compare towns that are similar except for the advisory body, and track outcomes over a longer period. On the evidence given, advisory bodies may improve economic outcomes if governments adopt and fund their recommendations, but the size of the effect is not yet established.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: the mechanisms are explained, the scenario is used to show the difference between correlation and causation, and the judgement is reasoned and qualified.

sampleAnswers.answer: The advisory body shares local knowledge, which can make the program more suitable. Employment rose faster in Town A, so the advisory body probably helped, but the towns are different, so this is not certain.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A 4-mark response analyses one mechanism with some accuracy, but the judgement is not developed and the comparison is only partly examined.

sampleAnswers.answer: Advisory bodies give advice, and employment rose more in Town A.

dotPoints.description: Governments as social welfare-maximising agents, including improving quality of life

prompts.question: Explain how the government could use the aim of maximising social welfare to choose between the two projects in the scenario.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: The government of Valdoria must choose between two projects that cost the same amount. Project one is a new public library in a suburb where most households are high-income and already have access to private resources. Project two is a free school breakfast program in a district where many children arrive at school without eating, and neither project would be provided by a private business.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Explains clearly that social welfare is maximised by choosing the option with the greatest total benefit to society, compares the benefit to each group in the scenario and reaches a reasoned choice
3 marks: Explains the principle of maximising social welfare and applies it to both projects with some accuracy
2 marks: Describes social welfare or the two projects with some accuracy and limited application
1 mark: Makes a general statement about government choices
markerNotes: Reward a response that defines social welfare as the total benefit to society, not the benefit to the government's budget
Credit an explicit comparison of who gains from each project, since this shows how the principle is applied
commonStudentErrors: Choosing the library because it is more popular with households, without considering whether the benefit to each household is larger
Treating social welfare as the same thing as government revenue or profit

sampleAnswers.answer: A social welfare-maximising government chooses the option that gives the greatest total benefit to society, counting the benefits to every group and not only the revenue or profit a project might earn. The library benefits households that can already afford private resources, so its additional benefit to society is likely to be smaller than that of the breakfast program. The breakfast program improves the quality of life of children who would otherwise go hungry at school, and it may also improve learning and equity between districts. Because both projects cost the same, the government would choose the breakfast program, provided its benefits are reasonably large.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: social welfare is defined as total benefit, each project is compared by group, and the choice follows from the principle.

sampleAnswers.answer: The government counts the benefits to society, so the breakfast program helps more children who would otherwise go hungry.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A 2-mark response describes the principle with some accuracy but compares the projects only briefly.

sampleAnswers.answer: The government should choose the project that is best for people.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A 1-mark response makes a general statement without applying the principle.

prompts.question: Discuss the extent to which a social welfare-maximising government should prioritise quality of life over allocative efficiency when choosing between the two options in the scenario.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A state government has $100 million to spend. Option A is a public transport upgrade that would cut average commuting time for households by 10 per cent and reduce vehicle emissions. Option B is a $100 million cut in the fuel tax, which would raise household disposable income by a similar amount but would increase emissions and encourage more driving. Advisers disagree on whether improving quality of life requires the government to focus on equity or on efficiency.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Discusses the extent to which quality of life should take priority over allocative efficiency, weighing the social welfare effects, equity and external costs of each option, and reaches a reasoned judgement
5 marks: Discusses the priority with accurate reference to both options and at least one effect on equity or external costs, with a conclusion
4 marks: Discusses the trade-off between quality of life and efficiency with some accuracy and a link to the options
3 marks: Describes social welfare or allocative efficiency with some accuracy and limited link to the scenario
2 marks: Identifies a feature of one option with a basic link to quality of life
1 mark: Makes a general statement about government spending
markerNotes: Reward responses that weigh the total benefit of each option, rather than the size of a single gain
Credit a judgement that depends on the scenario, such as the emissions cost of the fuel tax cut
commonStudentErrors: Assuming the option with the largest direct benefit to drivers always maximises social welfare
Equating allocative efficiency with equity, when an efficient outcome can still be unequal

sampleAnswers.answer: A social welfare-maximising government compares the total benefit of each option, including effects that do not appear in its accounts. Option A reduces commuting time for households, which improves quality of life for many people, and it lowers vehicle emissions, which reduces an external cost that the market does not price. Option B gives households a similar amount of disposable income, but it increases emissions and encourages driving, so part of the gain is offset by external costs. Allocative efficiency asks whether resources go where they produce the most benefit, and on the evidence given Option A is the more efficient. Equity matters too: a fuel tax cut benefits drivers in proportion to how much they drive, and public transport may be used more by lower-income households, so the equity effect depends on who uses each service. Quality of life should not automatically take priority over efficiency, because a less efficient choice leaves fewer resources for other goals. On balance, the government should favour Option A, provided its benefits are measured carefully rather than assumed.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: both options are weighed on total benefit, the equity and efficiency effects are separated, and the judgement rests on the scenario.

sampleAnswers.answer: Option A improves quality of life through shorter commutes and lower emissions. Option B gives households more income, but it increases emissions. The government should compare the two options on total benefits and costs, not on the gain to one group.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A 4-mark response discusses the trade-off with some accuracy and a link to the options, but does not weigh equity or efficiency in depth.

sampleAnswers.answer: Option A reduces commuting time, which improves quality of life.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A 2-mark response identifies one feature of one option with a basic link to quality of life.

dotPoints.description: Features of the Australian federal Budget and tax-transfer system

prompts.question: Outline the features of the federal Budget and the tax-transfer system shown in the scenario.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: In a hypothetical federal Budget, the government forecasts total revenue of $450 billion and total expenditure of $480 billion for the financial year. Personal income tax rates rise with income, and the age pension, which is a transfer payment, is paid to older people who meet income and asset tests.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Outlines the features of the federal Budget, including the budget deficit, and of the tax-transfer system, including progressive tax and transfer payments, with a clear link between them
3 marks: Outlines three features of the Budget or the tax-transfer system with accurate detail
2 marks: Identifies two features of the Budget or the tax-transfer system with limited explanation
1 mark: Identifies one feature of the federal Budget or the tax-transfer system
markerNotes: Reward responses that convert the figures into a budget deficit of $30 billion and explain what the deficit means
Credit a link between progressive tax, transfer payments and the redistribution of disposable income
commonStudentErrors: Describing the Budget as a single payment or one-off tax, rather than an annual statement of revenue and expenditure
Stating that a budget deficit means the government has more money than it spends

sampleAnswers.answer: The federal Budget is the government's annual statement of expected revenue and expenditure for the financial year. In this hypothetical Budget, revenue of $450 billion and expenditure of $480 billion produce a budget deficit of $30 billion, because spending exceeds revenue. The tax-transfer system works through personal income tax, which is progressive, so people with higher incomes pay a higher average rate. Transfer payments such as the age pension raise the disposable income of eligible older people, so the two parts of the system together redistribute income.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: the Budget and the tax-transfer system are both outlined, the deficit is calculated, and the link between progressive tax and transfers is explained.

sampleAnswers.answer: The Budget is an annual statement of revenue and expenditure, and this one shows a deficit.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A 2-mark response identifies two features with limited explanation and no use of the tax-transfer system.

sampleAnswers.answer: Income tax is a feature of the tax system.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A 1-mark response identifies one feature without explanation.

prompts.question: Analyse how the tax-transfer system acts as an automatic stabiliser in the downturn described in the scenario.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: Before a downturn, the federal Budget is in balance, with revenue and expenditure both at $100 billion. In the downturn, personal income tax receipts fall by $10 billion and spending on income support rises by $6 billion, with no change in government policy. Revenue from other sources and spending on other programs stay at their previous levels.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Analyses in a sustained way how falling tax receipts and rising transfers automatically move the budget towards deficit and limit the fall in disposable income, using the figures and reaching a reasoned conclusion on the limits of the stabiliser
5 marks: Analyses the automatic stabiliser effect with accurate use of the figures and at least one limitation
4 marks: Explains how the tax and transfer changes affect the budget balance with some accuracy and a link to the scenario
3 marks: Describes a tax or transfer change in the downturn with some accuracy
2 marks: Identifies income tax or transfer payments with a basic link to the downturn
1 mark: Makes a general statement about the budget in a downturn
markerNotes: Reward accurate arithmetic: the budget moves from zero to a deficit of $16 billion, because revenue falls by $10 billion and expenditure rises by $6 billion
Credit a limitation, such as the stabiliser working only within the existing tax and transfer rules, or a deficit that adds to public debt
commonStudentErrors: Adding the $10 billion and $6 billion as if they were both increases in expenditure
Describing the stabiliser as a discretionary policy change made by government

sampleAnswers.answer: The tax-transfer system acts as an automatic stabiliser because its components change with the economy without any new policy decision. Before the downturn the federal Budget is in balance, with revenue and expenditure both at $100 billion. Personal income tax receipts fall by $10 billion as incomes drop, so revenue falls to $90 billion. Spending on income support rises by $6 billion as more people qualify, so expenditure rises to $106 billion. The budget balance therefore moves from zero to a deficit of $16 billion, which adds to demand when private spending is falling. The stabiliser also limits the fall in disposable income, because transfers replace part of the lost income. Its effect is limited, however, because the size of the response is fixed by the existing rules, and a larger deficit must be financed. The deficit is a consequence of the downturn, not a policy choice.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: the calculations are accurate, the automatic nature of the stabiliser is explained, and a limitation is identified.

sampleAnswers.answer: Income tax falls and income support rises during the downturn, so the budget moves into deficit without any new policy. This helps to support disposable income.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A 4-mark response explains the effect on the budget balance with some accuracy but does not use the figures in full.

sampleAnswers.answer: Income support rises in a downturn, which increases spending.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A 2-mark response identifies one transfer with a basic link to the downturn.

dotPoints.description: Regulation as a government tool to manage the economy and minimise, mitigate or eliminate harm

prompts.question: Classify each of the three regulations in the scenario as minimising, mitigating or eliminating harm, and give a reason for each.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: The government of Valdoria introduces three regulations. It bans a food additive that has been shown to cause serious allergic reactions. It sets a maximum level of emissions that factories may release into the air. It requires a warning label on sugary drinks that shows how much sugar each serving contains, but the drinks may still be sold.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Classifies all three regulations correctly, with a specific reason for each that explains how the regulation limits the harm
2 marks: Classifies two regulations correctly, with a brief reason for each
1 mark: Classifies one regulation correctly or makes a general statement about regulation
markerNotes: Reward classifications that state the mechanism: a ban removes the product, a cap limits the amount of pollution, and a label informs choice without removing the product
Credit recognition that a cap can minimise harm without eliminating it, since some emissions still occur
commonStudentErrors: Classifying the warning label as eliminating harm because consumers are informed of the risk
Calling the emissions cap an elimination of harm because factories must comply with it

sampleAnswers.answer: Each regulation is classified by how far it reduces harm. The ban on the additive will eliminate harm entirely, because the product can no longer be sold. The emissions cap helps to minimise harm, since it reduces the pollution that factories release without stopping production. The warning label will mitigate harm by giving consumers information about sugar content, but the drinks can still be sold.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: all three regulations are classified correctly, and each reason explains how the regulation limits the harm.

sampleAnswers.answer: The ban eliminates harm from the additive, and the emissions cap reduces pollution.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A 2-mark response classifies two regulations, but the reasons are brief.

sampleAnswers.answer: The ban is a regulation that stops harm.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A 1-mark response classifies one regulation without a reason for the other two.

prompts.question: Assess whether regulation is the most effective way for government to minimise harm in the economy, compared with taxation.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A state government wants to reduce harm from an industrial chemical used by a local manufacturing industry. Option 1 is a total ban, which would close two factories and cost 400 jobs. Option 2 is a strict handling standard, enforced by inspectors, that factories can meet at a higher cost. Option 3 is a tax on the chemical equal to the estimated cost of the health damage it causes.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Assesses the effectiveness of regulation compared with taxation with sustained analysis of the three options, weighing the certainty of the harm reduction against the costs, and reaches a reasoned judgement
5 marks: Assesses regulation and taxation with accurate reference to at least two options and a clear comparison of their effectiveness
4 marks: Analyses the strengths or weaknesses of regulation or taxation with some accuracy and a link to the scenario
3 marks: Describes a regulation or a tax with some accuracy and limited comparison
2 marks: Identifies a feature of one option with a basic link to harm
1 mark: Makes a general statement about regulation
markerNotes: Reward a comparison that sets the certainty of regulation against the flexibility of a tax, rather than listing the features of each
Credit a judgement that depends on the type of harm, such as whether it is severe enough to justify a ban
commonStudentErrors: Claiming that a tax always reduces harm more than regulation, without evidence
Ignoring the job losses from the total ban when assessing its effectiveness

sampleAnswers.answer: Regulation is effective where the harm is serious and government must be certain of the result. A total ban, such as Option 1, can eliminate the harm entirely, but it would close two factories and cost 400 jobs, so the government would need to weigh that cost. A strict handling standard, Option 2, is a regulation that can minimise harm without closing the industry, but its effectiveness depends on inspectors and on factories meeting the standard at a higher cost. Where harm cannot be eliminated, such a standard can mitigate it. Taxation, in Option 3, works through price: a tax equal to the health damage makes factories pay for the harm they cause, so they can choose how to reduce it, which may achieve a lower total cost than a ban. However, the tax relies on an estimate of the damage, which may be wrong, and it does not guarantee that the harm will fall. On balance, regulation is the most effective choice where the harm is severe and must be eliminated, while taxation is more effective where the damage can be measured and firms should be free to respond.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: regulation and taxation are compared on certainty and cost, the limits of the damage estimate are weighed, and the judgement depends on the type of harm.

sampleAnswers.answer: Regulation can eliminate harm, as a ban would, but it may close factories and cost jobs. A tax lets firms choose how to reduce harm, but the estimate of the damage may be wrong.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A 4-mark response analyses the strengths and weaknesses of both approaches with some accuracy but does not reach a judgement.

sampleAnswers.answer: A ban can eliminate harm but would cost jobs.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A 2-mark response identifies one feature of one option with a basic link to harm.

dotPoints.description: Government use of nudges and incentives to alter the economic behaviour of households and businesses

prompts.question: Classify each of the four measures in the scenario as a nudge or an incentive, giving a reason for each.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A state government introduces four measures. It pays a $200 rebate to households that install a solar hot-water system. New employees are automatically enrolled in a retirement savings plan, with the option to opt out. New cars must display a label showing the annual running cost of the vehicle. Businesses that buy low-emission delivery vans receive a tax concession of $5,000 per van.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Classifies each measure correctly as a nudge or an incentive, with a reason that explains how it changes the economic behaviour of households or businesses
3 marks: Classifies three measures correctly, with a reason for each
2 marks: Classifies two measures correctly, with limited reasoning
1 mark: Classifies one measure correctly or makes a general statement about nudges
markerNotes: Reward a classification that names the mechanism, such as a default changing choices without removing any option, rather than a bare label
Credit recognition that incentives change the cost or payoff of a choice, while nudges change the way choices are presented
commonStudentErrors: Classifying the automatic enrolment as an incentive because it gives workers a retirement benefit
Calling the rebate a nudge because it makes households more aware of solar energy

sampleAnswers.answer: Nudges change the way choices are presented, while incentives change their cost. The $200 rebate is an incentive, because it lowers the cost of a solar hot-water system and so changes the economic behaviour of households. Automatic enrolment with an option to opt out is a nudge, because it changes the default option without removing any choice. The running-cost label is also a nudge, since it presents information in a simple form that may influence buyers without changing any price. The tax concession is an incentive, because it reduces the cost of low-emission vans and so changes the economic behaviour of businesses.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: each measure is classified correctly, and the reasons explain the mechanism for households and businesses.

sampleAnswers.answer: The rebate is an incentive, and the automatic enrolment is a nudge.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A 2-mark response classifies two measures correctly without explaining the mechanism.

sampleAnswers.answer: The rebate is an incentive for households.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A 1-mark response classifies one measure correctly without any reasoning.

prompts.question: Assess the view that nudges are more effective than incentives at changing the economic behaviour of households and businesses.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A city council trialled two approaches to increase recycling by households. In Area A, households received a letter showing how their recycling rate compared with their neighbours', and the rate rose by 4 percentage points over one year. In Area B, households received a $50 credit on their rates for each month they recycled at least 80 per cent of their waste, and the rate rose by 7 percentage points over the same year. The areas differ in household income, and the council did not use a control area. Local businesses were also offered a rebate for recyclable packaging, but this was not evaluated.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Assesses the view with sustained analysis of how nudges and incentives work, weighing the trial results, the limits of the evidence and the cost of each approach, and reaches a reasoned judgement
5 marks: Assesses the view with accurate reference to both approaches and the trial results, with at least one limitation and a conclusion
4 marks: Analyses the difference between nudges and incentives with some accuracy and a link to the scenario
3 marks: Describes a nudge or an incentive with some accuracy and limited comparison
2 marks: Identifies a feature of one approach with a basic link to behaviour
1 mark: Makes a general statement about recycling or behaviour change
markerNotes: Reward a judgement that the trial cannot show which approach is more effective, because the areas differ and there is no control
Credit a cost comparison, since a monthly credit is a recurring cost while a letter is cheap to send
commonStudentErrors: Concluding that incentives are more effective because Area B's rate rose by more, without noting that the areas differ
Assuming a nudge changes behaviour permanently, without considering whether the effect lasts

sampleAnswers.answer: The view is not supported by the trial alone. Nudges, such as the neighbour comparison letter, change behaviour by informing households about social norms without changing their financial position, so they can be cheap to deliver. Incentives, such as the $50 monthly credit, change economic behaviour by altering the payoff for recycling, which can produce larger effects but at a recurring cost to the council. Area B's recycling rate rose by 7 percentage points against 4 in Area A, a difference of 3 percentage points, but this is a correlation rather than proof of causation. The areas differ in household income, and the council used no control area, so the difference may reflect those factors. The rebate for businesses was not evaluated and cannot be used in the judgement. A stronger test would compare matched areas over a longer period and measure the cost per percentage point gained. On the evidence given, incentives may achieve larger changes, but nudges may be more cost-effective, and the claim that nudges are more effective cannot be confirmed.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: the two approaches are explained, the trial is read with attention to correlation and causation, and the judgement is qualified by cost and evidence.

sampleAnswers.answer: A nudge, like the letter, changes behaviour by informing households about what neighbours do. An incentive, like the credit, changes the payoff. The trial shows a larger rise in Area B, but the areas differ, so the evidence is limited.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A 4-mark response analyses the difference between nudges and incentives with some accuracy but does not weigh the cost or the evidence.

sampleAnswers.answer: The letter is a nudge and the credit is an incentive.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A 2-mark response identifies one feature of each approach without a link to behaviour.

dotPoints.description: Arguments for and against the privatisation and nationalisation of businesses

prompts.question: Outline one argument for and one argument against the privatisation of the water utility described in the scenario, and state how the position would change under nationalisation.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A state-owned water utility supplies 1.2 million households and pays its annual profit to the state government. The government is considering selling the utility to a private company, which would be regulated by an independent price regulator.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Outlines a clear argument for and against privatisation, linked to the water utility, and explains how public ownership under nationalisation would change the trade-off between profit and public service
3 marks: Outlines an argument for and against privatisation with accurate reasons linked to the scenario
2 marks: Identifies an argument for or against privatisation with limited explanation
1 mark: Makes a general statement about privatisation or nationalisation
markerNotes: Reward an argument tied to the water utility, such as the profit incentive or the natural monopoly, rather than a general list
Credit a clear statement that nationalisation keeps the profit with government but may reduce the pressure to cut costs
commonStudentErrors: Stating that privatisation always lowers prices for households, without regard to the price regulator
Assuming that nationalisation means the business must make losses

sampleAnswers.answer: One argument for privatisation of the utility is that a private owner has a profit incentive to cut costs and invest efficiently, which may lower the cost of supplying water to households. One argument against is that water supply is a natural monopoly, so a private owner could charge high prices unless the independent price regulator controls them, and the government would lose the annual profit it currently receives. Under nationalisation, the profit would stay with government and the utility could focus on public service, but the pressure to cut costs that competition and profit provide would be weaker. The choice depends on how well the regulator or the government can make these businesses serve the public.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: one argument for and one against are outlined and linked to the utility, and the change under nationalisation is explained.

sampleAnswers.answer: A private owner may cut costs to make a profit, which could lower prices.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A 2-mark response identifies one argument for privatisation with limited explanation.

sampleAnswers.answer: Privatisation means selling a business to private owners.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A 1-mark response makes a general statement about privatisation.

prompts.question: Discuss whether nationalisation or privatisation is more likely to serve the public interest where a business is a natural monopoly, using the regional rail network in the scenario.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A state government is reviewing its regional rail network, which is a natural monopoly. The network carries 60,000 passengers a day across the region, but it loses money on some routes that serve small towns. The options are to keep the network in public ownership through nationalisation of a private operator that has run into financial difficulty, or to sell it to a private company under a long-term contract that requires service on the unprofitable routes.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Discusses whether nationalisation or privatisation better serves the public interest, with sustained analysis of efficiency, service on unprofitable routes and the role of regulation, and reaches a reasoned conclusion
5 marks: Discusses both options with accurate reference to the natural monopoly and the scenario, and makes a conclusion
4 marks: Discusses one or both options with some accuracy and a link to the scenario
3 marks: Describes an argument for nationalisation or privatisation with some accuracy and limited link to the scenario
2 marks: Identifies a feature of one option with a basic reference to the scenario
1 mark: Makes a general statement about rail services
markerNotes: Reward an analysis that explains why a natural monopoly makes competition unlikely, so the choice rests on regulation or public ownership
Credit a conclusion that addresses the unprofitable routes, since a private owner may leave them unserved unless a contract requires otherwise
commonStudentErrors: Claiming that competition will develop in a rail network that is a natural monopoly
Treating profit as the only measure of the public interest

sampleAnswers.answer: Where a business is a natural monopoly, competition is unlikely to discipline prices or service, so the choice between privatisation and nationalisation depends on the regulation and ownership the government can secure. Privatisation may bring efficiency gains, since a private operator has a profit incentive to cut costs, and a sale can reduce the government's exposure to losses on the network. However, the network loses money on some routes, and a private owner will tend to reduce or close services on those routes unless a contract requires otherwise, which weakens the public interest. Nationalisation keeps the network in public ownership, so government can set service levels on unprofitable routes and keep fares affordable, but public ownership may reduce the pressure to lower costs if the businesses are funded without strict performance targets. The 60,000 daily passengers show that the network serves a large population. On balance, public ownership is more likely to serve the public interest where the network is a natural monopoly, provided government sets clear performance targets for the businesses it runs.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: the natural monopoly is used to frame the choice, both options are weighed against service on unprofitable routes, and the conclusion is qualified.

sampleAnswers.answer: A private owner may cut costs, but it may also close routes that lose money, so the public interest may suffer. Public ownership protects service but may reduce the pressure to cut costs.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A 4-mark response discusses both options with some accuracy but does not link the natural monopoly to the choice.

sampleAnswers.answer: A private owner would want to make a profit on the rail network.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A 2-mark response identifies one feature of one option with a basic reference to the scenario.

dotPoints.description: Purposes of taxation for the economy and society

prompts.question: Describe the purpose of taxation illustrated by each of the three measures in the scenario.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: The government of Valdoria introduces three measures. It adds a tax to tobacco products to discourage smoking, uses income tax revenue to fund public schools, and raises the top tax rate on high-income earners to fund an increase in the age pension.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Describes the purpose of taxation illustrated by all three measures, linking each to its effect on the economy or society, with a clear reason
3 marks: Describes the purpose of taxation for all three measures with some accuracy
2 marks: Describes two purposes of taxation with limited explanation
1 mark: Identifies one purpose of taxation
markerNotes: Reward responses that name the purpose of each measure (behaviour change, revenue, redistribution) and tie it to the economy or society
Credit recognition that one tax can serve more than one purpose, such as the tobacco tax raising revenue as well as discouraging smoking
commonStudentErrors: Describing the income tax for schools as redistribution because everyone pays it
Calling the tobacco tax a purpose of raising revenue only, without identifying its effect on behaviour

sampleAnswers.answer: The purposes of taxation illustrated here are behaviour change, revenue raising and redistribution. The tobacco tax changes behaviour: by raising the price of tobacco products it discourages smoking, which reduces harm to society and lowers the cost to the economy of smoking-related illness. Income tax revenue used to fund public schools serves a revenue purpose, since it pays for a service that the government provides to the whole of society. Raising the top tax rate to fund the age pension serves a redistribution purpose, because income is moved from high-income earners to older people with lower incomes.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: each measure is matched to a purpose of taxation, and each is linked to its effect on the economy or society.

sampleAnswers.answer: The tobacco tax discourages smoking, and the income tax funds public schools.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A 2-mark response identifies two purposes with limited explanation and omits the redistribution measure.

sampleAnswers.answer: Income tax raises revenue for the government.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A 1-mark response identifies one purpose without describing how it applies to the scenario.

prompts.question: Discuss the trade-offs that government faces when a single tax, such as the proposed tax on sugary drinks, is used for more than one of the purposes of taxation.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A government considers a tax on sugary drinks. The tax would raise $300 million a year in revenue, is forecast to reduce consumption of sugary drinks by 10 per cent, and would fall most heavily on low-income households. Some industry groups argue that it would cost jobs at local bottling plants.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Discusses a clear trade-off between the purposes of taxation, with sustained analysis of the revenue, behaviour and equity effects in the scenario, weighing the forecasts and reaching a reasoned conclusion
5 marks: Discusses at least two trade-offs with accurate reference to the scenario, with a conclusion
4 marks: Discusses one trade-off with some accuracy and a link to the scenario
3 marks: Describes two purposes of taxation with some accuracy and limited link to the trade-off
2 marks: Identifies a purpose of taxation with a basic reference to the scenario
1 mark: Makes a general statement about taxes
markerNotes: Reward recognition that a tax that changes behaviour may raise less revenue over time, so the purposes can conflict
Credit the point that the 10 per cent fall is a forecast, and that any link between the tax and jobs needs evidence
commonStudentErrors: Assuming the 10 per cent fall in consumption is certain rather than a forecast
Describing the tax as unfair without explaining why low-income households pay a larger share of their income on it

sampleAnswers.answer: The purposes of taxation can conflict in a single tax, creating a clear trade-off. The sugary drinks tax raises $300 million a year in revenue, which can fund services that benefit society, but that revenue falls as the tax succeeds in changing behaviour. The forecast 10 per cent fall in consumption is an estimate, so the revenue and the behaviour-change effect cannot both be relied on in the budget. The tax also has a redistribution effect: because low-income households spend a larger share of their income on sugary drinks, the tax falls most heavily on them, which conflicts with the goal of fairness in society. Some industry groups argue that the tax will cost jobs at local bottling plants, a cost to the economy that the forecast may not capture. Government can reduce the regressive effect by returning part of the revenue to low-income households, but this reduces the revenue available for other purposes. On balance, the tax is justified if the health benefits of lower consumption outweigh the cost to low-income households and the risk to jobs, and government should test these claims against evidence before deciding.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: the trade-off between revenue and behaviour change is explained, the equity and jobs effects are weighed, and the conclusion depends on the evidence.

sampleAnswers.answer: The tax raises revenue, but if consumption falls the revenue falls too, so the purposes conflict. It also falls most heavily on low-income households, which is a redistribution cost to weigh.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A 4-mark response discusses one trade-off with some accuracy but does not reach a conclusion.

sampleAnswers.answer: The tax raises revenue and discourages consumption of sugary drinks.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A 2-mark response identifies a purpose with a basic reference to the scenario.

dotPoints.description: Major sources of Australian Government revenue

prompts.question: Outline the three largest major sources of Australian Government revenue in the scenario, and state the share of total revenue that personal income tax provides.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: In a hypothetical year, the Australian Government collects total revenue of $100 billion. Personal income tax provides $50 billion, company tax provides $18 billion, the goods and services tax (GST) provides $30 billion, and other sources provide $2 billion.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Outlines the three largest major sources of revenue correctly, with their amounts or relative size, and states the 50 per cent share from personal income tax
2 marks: Outlines two major sources of revenue, or names three with limited detail
1 mark: Identifies one source of Australian Government revenue
markerNotes: Reward answers that give the amounts or the shares, and that state the share of personal income tax as 50 per cent of the $100 billion total
Credit a clear statement that GST is a consumption tax, distinct from taxes on income
commonStudentErrors: Listing other things, such as the budget deficit, as sources of revenue
Calculating the personal income tax share against expenditure instead of total revenue

sampleAnswers.answer: The three largest major sources of Australian Government revenue in the scenario are personal income tax, which provides $50 billion, the goods and services tax (GST), which provides $30 billion, and company tax, which provides $18 billion. Personal income tax provides 50 per cent of total revenue of $100 billion.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: the three largest sources are identified with their amounts, and the 50 per cent share is calculated correctly.

sampleAnswers.answer: Personal income tax and GST are major sources of revenue for the government.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A 2-mark response names two sources without amounts or the share.

sampleAnswers.answer: Personal income tax is a source of revenue.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A 1-mark response identifies one source of revenue.

prompts.question: Analyse how a fall in tax receipts during the downturn described in the scenario changes the major sources of Australian Government revenue and the budget balance.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: In a downturn, personal income tax falls by 20 per cent, from $50 billion to $40 billion, and company tax falls by 25 per cent, from $18 billion to $13.5 billion. GST falls by 5 per cent, from $30 billion to $28.5 billion, and other sources stay at $2 billion. Government expenditure stays at $100 billion, the same as before the downturn, when revenue was also $100 billion.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Analyses in a sustained way how the fall in each source changes the composition of revenue and the budget balance, using the calculated shares and deficit, and explains why GST's share rises
5 marks: Analyses the change in revenue and the budget balance with accurate calculations and a comparison of shares
4 marks: Analyses the fall in one or two sources with accurate calculations and a link to the budget balance
3 marks: Describes the change in revenue with some accuracy and limited calculation
2 marks: Identifies a source of revenue that falls, with a basic link to the scenario
1 mark: Makes a general statement about the economy in a downturn
markerNotes: Reward accurate calculations: total revenue falls to $84 billion, a fall of 16 per cent, producing a deficit of $16 billion
Credit recognition that GST's share rises because its fall is smaller than the falls in income-based taxes
commonStudentErrors: Calculating the post-downturn shares using the pre-downturn total of $100 billion
Stating that the 16 per cent fall applies to income tax alone, when it is the fall in total revenue

sampleAnswers.answer: Total revenue falls from $100 billion to $84 billion, a fall of 16 per cent, because personal income tax falls by $10 billion, company tax by $4.5 billion and GST by $1.5 billion. The major sources of Australian Government revenue therefore change in composition as well as in size. Personal income tax falls from 50 per cent of revenue to about 47.6 per cent (40 divided by 84), and company tax falls from 18 per cent to about 16.1 per cent (13.5 divided by 84). GST rises from 30 per cent to about 33.9 per cent (28.5 divided by 84), because its fall of 5 per cent is smaller than the falls in the income-based taxes. Expenditure is unchanged at $100 billion, so the budget balance moves from zero to a deficit of $16 billion. The shares show that income-based taxes are more sensitive to the downturn than the GST, which is a consumption tax. These conclusions depend on the hypothetical rates of change and should not be read as a forecast for any real economy.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: the revenue total, the shares and the budget balance are all calculated correctly, and the change in composition is explained.

sampleAnswers.answer: Personal income tax falls by $10 billion and company tax by $4.5 billion, so total revenue falls. Expenditure does not change, so the budget moves into deficit.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A 4-mark response analyses the fall in two sources with accurate calculations but does not calculate the shares.

sampleAnswers.answer: Revenue falls in the downturn because income tax falls.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A 2-mark response identifies a source that falls with a basic link to the scenario.

dotPoints.description: Features of the tax base, including income, wealth and consumption

prompts.question: Outline the features of the income, wealth and consumption tax bases.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A state treasury paper lists three possible tax bases for raising revenue: the incomes that households and businesses earn, the value of land and other assets they own, and the spending they make on goods and services. The paper notes that each base behaves differently when the economy changes.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Outlines the features of income, wealth and consumption as tax bases, covering the size, stability and ease of collection of each base
3 marks: Outlines the features of at least two tax bases with accurate detail
2 marks: Identifies income, wealth or consumption as a tax base with a brief description
1 mark: Makes a general statement about taxation
markerNotes: Strong answers give one distinct feature for each base, such as the cyclical sensitivity of income or the difficulty of valuing wealth, rather than naming the bases only
Reward correct use of tax base to mean the thing being taxed, not the rate
commonStudentErrors: Confusing the tax base with the tax rate
Treating the three bases as having the same features

sampleAnswers.answer: Each tax base has features that affect the revenue it raises. The income base includes wages, salaries, interest and dividends. It is cyclical, rising and falling with employment and wage growth. The wealth base consists of property and other assets such as land and shares. Land cannot be moved, which makes wealth hard to avoid, but the value of assets that are rarely sold is difficult to measure. The consumption base is spending on goods and services. It is broad, simple to collect at the point of sale and less volatile than income, but it does not tax saving directly and can fall more heavily on low-income households.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Covers all three bases with a distinct, accurate feature of each, and uses the key terms precisely. It stays on outlining features without straying into policy judgements.

sampleAnswers.answer: Income is what people earn from their jobs, and the government taxes it. Wealth is property and shares that people own. Consumption is when people buy things.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies the three bases with brief description only. It gives no features such as stability or ease of collection, so it stays at the identification level.

sampleAnswers.answer: Governments tax income, wealth and spending to get money.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Makes a general statement about taxation. It does not outline features of the bases.

prompts.question: Analyse how the features of the income, wealth and consumption tax bases affect the stability of government revenue during a recession.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: In one year of recession, a national government finds that its revenue from taxes on wages and salaries falls by 12 per cent, its revenue from taxes on property and land falls by 4 per cent, and its revenue from taxes on spending on goods and services falls by 3 per cent. Its treasury wants to know which tax base gives the most stable revenue.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Analyses how the features of each tax base cause its revenue to respond differently in a recession, linking the cyclical income base, the asset-linked wealth base and the spending-linked consumption base to the stability of government revenue
5 marks: Analyses the stability of revenue from at least two tax bases with accurate reference to the features of each and to the scenario figures
4 marks: Explains how the features of the tax bases affect government revenue, with some accurate reference to the scenario
3 marks: Describes the difference between the income, wealth and consumption tax bases with some relevant detail
2 marks: Identifies one feature of a tax base with limited relevance to revenue stability
1 mark: Makes a general statement about government revenue
markerNotes: Strong answers link each base's feature to the scenario figures and explain the mechanism, such as falling wages reducing income tax collections
Reward recognition that the figures show a pattern and do not prove that one base is always more stable
commonStudentErrors: Stating the revenue fall without explaining why each base responds differently
Describing each tax base without linking it to revenue stability
Ignoring the percentage changes given in the scenario

sampleAnswers.answer: The stability of government revenue depends on how closely each tax base follows the economy. The features of the income base make it the most cyclical. Wages and salaries fall when employment falls, so income tax collections drop quickly, which is consistent with the 12 per cent fall in the scenario. The wealth base is linked to the value of land and other assets. Asset prices can change sharply, but they are not tied directly to the flow of income in a single year, which may explain the smaller 4 per cent fall. Consumption is linked to spending, and households tend to smooth their spending by drawing on savings, so the 3 per cent fall in consumption tax revenue is the smallest. A government that relies heavily on income tax is therefore most exposed to a recession, while a mix of bases spreads the risk. The result depends on the severity of the downturn and on the rates set for each base, so the data show a pattern rather than proof that one base is always more stable.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Analyses the features of all three bases and links each to the scenario figures with a reasoned conclusion. It also notes the limits of the evidence, which is what separates a sustained analysis from a list.

sampleAnswers.answer: Income tax falls in a recession because wages fall when people lose jobs. Property tax depends on property values, and consumption tax depends on spending. Both are less affected, so a government with more consumption tax has more stable revenue.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains the income base clearly, but the comparison with the other bases is vague and does not use the scenario figures.

sampleAnswers.answer: Income tax falls in a recession because people earn less. The other two taxes are steadier.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies a feature of the income base but does not explain the other bases or use the figures.

dotPoints.description: Types of taxation, including personal income, profit, sales taxes and excise duty

prompts.question: Classify each of the four taxes in the scenario as personal income, profit, sales or excise duty.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A government's revenue summary lists four taxes. (a) A tax withheld from the wages that employees earn. (b) A tax on the annual earnings of a company after its costs are deducted. (c) A tax of 8 per cent added to the price of most goods and services sold to consumers. (d) A tax of a fixed amount on each litre of fuel sold.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Classifies all four taxes correctly and gives a brief reason for each based on what is taxed
2 marks: Classifies at least two of the taxes correctly
1 mark: Identifies one type of tax correctly
markerNotes: Strong answers tie each tax to its base, such as earnings for personal income tax and quantity for excise duty, rather than naming the tax only
Reward accurate use of levied to describe what the tax applies to
commonStudentErrors: Calling the fuel tax a sales tax because it is paid at the point of sale
Confusing a profit tax with personal income tax on wages

sampleAnswers.answer: (a) is a personal income tax, levied on the earnings of individuals. (b) is a profit tax, levied on the surplus that a company earns after its costs. (c) is a sales tax: sales taxes are levied on the price of goods and services at the point of sale. (d) is an excise duty, a tax levied on a specific good at a set amount per unit.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Classifies all four correctly and gives a reason for each based on what is taxed. The reasons are brief, which is appropriate for the marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: (a) is a personal income tax and (b) is a profit tax. However, (c) and (d) are both excise duties because the government collects them.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Classifies two taxes correctly but misclassifies the sales tax as an excise duty. Excise duty applies to specific goods at a set amount, not to general sales.

sampleAnswers.answer: (a) is a personal income tax. The others are taxes that the government collects.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies one tax correctly but does not classify the rest. Saying the government collects them does not identify their type.

prompts.question: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of relying on excise duty rather than personal income tax as a source of government revenue.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A small island nation raises most of its revenue from personal income tax. A committee proposes raising excise duty on fuel, alcohol and tobacco and cutting personal income tax to compensate. Its advisers note that motorists have few short-run substitutes for fuel, so their demand changes little when the price rises.
prompts.markingCriteria:
5 marks: Discusses the advantages and disadvantages of excise duty and personal income tax for government revenue, using the scenario and the concept of elasticity to reach a reasoned view
4 marks: Discusses the advantages and disadvantages of both taxes with relevant reference to the scenario
3 marks: Explains one advantage and one disadvantage of excise duty or personal income tax with some accuracy
2 marks: Describes excise duty or personal income tax with limited accuracy
1 mark: Makes a general statement about government revenue
markerNotes: Strong answers weigh revenue gains against distributional effects and link the elasticity of fuel demand to the size of the revenue
Reward a reasoned view that states what the trade-off depends on
commonStudentErrors: Listing advantages without any disadvantages
Calling excise duty progressive because it is a tax on spending

sampleAnswers.answer: Excise duty is a tax on specific goods, usually charged per unit, so it is simple to collect because it applies to a small number of producers and importers. Its base is narrow, so revenue depends on the quantity sold rather than on income, and it does not rise automatically as incomes grow. Excise is also regressive, since low-income households spend a larger share of their income on fuel, alcohol and tobacco. Low elasticity of demand for fuel means a higher fuel excise would raise significant government revenue quickly, but the same feature makes the burden hard to avoid. Personal income tax has a broad base and can be progressive, so it reflects ability to pay, but it can reduce incentives to work. A reasoned view is that the committee should weigh the revenue gain against the regressive effects before shifting the burden.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Discusses both taxes on advantages and disadvantages and uses the elasticity point to support a reasoned view. The regressive effect is clearly linked to the goods taxed.

sampleAnswers.answer: Excise duty is easy to collect because it applies to few producers. However, it is regressive, because poorer households spend more of their income on fuel. Personal income tax has a broad base, which is an advantage.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Gives one advantage and one disadvantage of excise duty with some accuracy. It does not discuss the disadvantages of personal income tax or use elasticity.

sampleAnswers.answer: Excise duty is a tax on goods, and the government collects it.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Makes a general statement about excise duty without weighing advantages or disadvantages.

dotPoints.description: Characteristics and types of direct and indirect taxes, including the economic and legal incidence of tax

prompts.question: Define a direct tax and an indirect tax, using the two levies in the scenario as examples.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A government's budget papers describe two levies. One is withheld from employees' pay by their employers according to their earnings. The other is charged on each packet of cigarettes at the point of sale.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Defines direct and indirect taxes accurately and correctly uses both levies from the scenario as examples
2 marks: Defines a direct tax or an indirect tax accurately, or defines both with limited detail
1 mark: Makes a general statement about taxes
markerNotes: Strong answers name who is legally liable for each tax, which is the key difference between the two types
Reward correct use of the scenario levies as examples rather than general examples
commonStudentErrors: Defining direct tax as any tax paid by people
Stating that indirect taxes cannot be passed on to anyone

sampleAnswers.answer: A direct tax is levied on the income, wealth or profit of a person or business, and the legal liability rests with the taxpayer. The levy withheld from employees' pay is a direct tax. An indirect tax is levied on goods and services. The seller pays it to government, although the cost may be passed on to buyers. The charge on each packet of cigarettes is an indirect tax.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Defines both types accurately, names the legal liability and uses both levies as examples. The point about passing on costs shows understanding beyond the definition.

sampleAnswers.answer: A direct tax is paid on income. An indirect tax is paid on goods. The pay levy is direct and the cigarette charge is indirect.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Defines both types but with limited detail. It does not explain who is liable or how the cost may be passed on.

sampleAnswers.answer: Direct tax is a tax on people, and indirect tax is a tax on things.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Makes a general statement that does not define either type accurately.

prompts.question: Apply the concepts of economic incidence and legal incidence to explain how the burden of this tax is shared between consumers and wholesalers.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A government imposes a tax of 10 cents per litre on petrol, paid to government by fuel wholesalers. In the month after the tax begins, the pump price paid by motorists rises by 7 cents per litre, and the net price that wholesalers receive falls by 3 cents per litre. Motorists have few short-run substitutes for petrol, so their demand changes little when the price rises.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Applies legal and economic incidence to explain why consumers bear 70 per cent of the tax, linking the short-run elasticity of demand to the 7 cent price rise and the 3 cent fall in the wholesalers' net price
5 marks: Applies both forms of incidence accurately to the scenario with a clear reason for the sharing of the burden
4 marks: Applies the concept of economic incidence with some accurate reference to the scenario
3 marks: Explains legal incidence or economic incidence accurately without referring to the scenario
2 marks: Identifies legal or economic incidence with limited explanation
1 mark: Makes a general statement about taxes
markerNotes: Strong answers separate who pays the tax to government from who bears its cost, and show how the bearer depends on elasticity
Reward correct arithmetic: 7 of the 10 cents is 70 per cent, and 3 cents is 30 per cent
commonStudentErrors: Stating that the wholesalers bear the whole burden because they are the legal taxpayers
Confusing the legal incidence of a tax with its economic incidence

sampleAnswers.answer: Legal incidence is the question of who is legally required to pay the tax to government. Here the wholesalers are the legal taxpayers, because the levy is paid to government at the point of supply. Economic incidence is the question of who ultimately bears the cost, and this depends on how buyers and sellers respond to the tax, not on who pays it. Motorists have few short-run substitutes for petrol, so their demand changes little when the price rises. The 7 cent rise in the pump price shows that the price elasticity of demand is low relative to supply here, so consumers bear more of the burden. The wholesalers absorb the remaining 3 cents, since their net price falls. Consumers therefore bear 70 per cent of the burden and wholesalers 30 per cent, even though wholesalers are the legal taxpayers.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Applies both forms of incidence to the scenario, uses the figures correctly to show a 70 per cent consumer share, and links the result to elasticity. The distinction between legal and economic incidence is precise.

sampleAnswers.answer: Legal incidence is who pays the tax to government, which here is the wholesalers. Economic incidence is who bears the cost. Consumers pay more because petrol demand changes little when prices rise, so 7 cents of the 10 cents is passed on.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Applies both forms of incidence and reaches the right split, but the explanation of why consumers bear more is brief and does not refer to elasticity.

sampleAnswers.answer: The wholesalers pay the tax to government, so they are the legal payers. Consumers may also pay some of it through higher prices.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies legal incidence and notes that consumers may pay, but does not explain the economic incidence or use the figures.

dotPoints.description: Features of a good tax, including simplicity, fairness and efficiency

prompts.question: Describe what it means for a tax to be simple, using the proposal in the scenario as an example.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A government proposes replacing 14 separate charges paid by small businesses with one annual turnover tax of 1 per cent of each business's turnover, applied at the same rate to all businesses regardless of profit.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Describes simplicity accurately, explaining how fewer rates and rules lower compliance costs and make the tax easy to understand, with a correct example from the scenario
2 marks: Describes simplicity with some accuracy but gives little or no reference to the scenario
1 mark: Makes a general statement about tax simplicity
markerNotes: Strong answers explain simplicity in terms of compliance costs and administration, not just that the tax is easy
Reward use of the scenario, such as replacing 14 charges with one rate
commonStudentErrors: Equating simplicity with a low tax rate
Describing simplicity without saying who benefits, the taxpayer or the government

sampleAnswers.answer: Simplicity means that a tax is easy for taxpayers to understand and calculate, with few rates, few exemptions and low compliance costs. The proposal would replace 14 charges with one rate of 1 per cent of turnover, so a business could work out its liability with a single calculation. Simplicity also reduces the cost of administration for the government, since fewer rules mean less auditing and fewer disputes.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes simplicity accurately for both taxpayers and the government, and applies it to the scenario with a correct example.

sampleAnswers.answer: A simple tax has one rate, so it is easy to calculate. The proposal has one rate of 1 per cent.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes simplicity with some accuracy and refers to the scenario, but does not explain compliance costs or administration.

sampleAnswers.answer: A simple tax is easy to understand.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Makes a general statement about simplicity without description or reference to the scenario.

prompts.question: Justify whether the turnover tax in the scenario is a good tax, judging it against simplicity, fairness and efficiency.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A government replaces 14 separate small-business charges with a single annual turnover tax of 1 per cent of each business's turnover, applied at the same rate to all businesses regardless of profit. A business with $1 million turnover and $100,000 profit pays $10,000, while a business with $200,000 turnover and $50,000 profit pays $2,000.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Justifies a clear judgement on whether the turnover tax is a good tax, weighing simplicity, fairness and efficiency with specific reference to the scenario figures
5 marks: Justifies a judgement with accurate reference to at least two of simplicity, fairness and efficiency
4 marks: Discusses the features of the tax with some relevant reference to the scenario
3 marks: Describes one feature of a good tax with some accuracy
2 marks: Identifies simplicity, fairness or efficiency with limited explanation
1 mark: Makes a general statement about taxes
markerNotes: Strong answers use the scenario figures, such as the tax as a share of profit, to test fairness
Reward a judgement that is reasoned against the three criteria, not a list of features
commonStudentErrors: Treating fairness only as equal rates, without considering ability to pay
Claiming that a tax on turnover is efficient because it is simple to collect

sampleAnswers.answer: On simplicity, the turnover tax scores well. One rate, one base and few exemptions mean that compliance costs would be low, and businesses could calculate the charge easily. On fairness, it treats businesses equally, since every business faces the same rate, which is horizontal equity. However, it does not reflect ability to pay. The business with $1 million turnover and $100,000 profit pays $10,000, which is 10 per cent of its profit, while the business with $200,000 turnover and $50,000 profit pays $2,000, which is 4 per cent of its profit. Firms with thin margins carry a heavier burden relative to what they earn, a serious vertical inequity. On efficiency, a tax on turnover does not depend on profit, so it does not discourage production directly, but it may encourage firms to reorganise to reduce measured turnover. On balance, the tax is simple and reasonably efficient, but its weakness on fairness is serious, so it is not a good tax unless the base or rate is adjusted to reflect profit.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Makes a clear judgement and tests fairness with the scenario figures, showing the 10 and 4 per cent shares of profit. The efficiency point is recognised as a possible behavioural response, not a certainty.

sampleAnswers.answer: The turnover tax is simple because there is only one rate, so businesses can calculate it easily. It treats all businesses the same, which is fair. However, it does not depend on profit, so businesses with low profit margins may face an unfair burden.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Discusses simplicity and fairness with some reference to the scenario, but the claim that equal treatment is fair is not developed and efficiency is not addressed.

sampleAnswers.answer: It is simple because there is one rate. It might not be fair to some businesses.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies simplicity and a fairness concern with limited explanation. It does not use the scenario figures or reach a judgement.

dotPoints.description: Rationale for reform of the Australian taxation system

prompts.question: Outline two reasons for reform of the Australian taxation system, using the scenario.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A government's budget paper reports three trends. Tax thresholds have not been adjusted for several years, so rising nominal wages move more people into higher tax brackets. Revenue from company profits and commodity-related income has varied sharply from year to year. The population is ageing, so spending on pensions and health care is rising.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Outlines two reasons for reform of the Australian taxation system, with accurate explanation of how each trend in the scenario affects revenue or taxpayers
3 marks: Outlines one reason for reform with accurate explanation and some reference to the scenario
2 marks: Identifies a reason for reform of the taxation system with limited explanation
1 mark: Makes a general statement about taxation
markerNotes: Strong answers explain the mechanism behind each reason, such as unindexed thresholds raising the effective tax rate
Reward reference to specific trends in the scenario rather than generic reasons
commonStudentErrors: Stating that tax reform is needed because taxes are high, without a mechanism
Describing the trends without explaining why they justify reform

sampleAnswers.answer: Two reasons stand out for reform of the Australian taxation system. The first is bracket creep, or fiscal drag. When nominal wages rise with inflation but tax thresholds are not adjusted, more people move into higher brackets, so the effective tax rate rises without any change in legislation. The second is volatile revenue. If collections depend heavily on company profits and commodity-related income, government revenue becomes unstable, and a broader base would reduce that risk.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Outlines two reasons, each with an accurate mechanism drawn from the scenario. It uses the terms precisely and stays within the outline task.

sampleAnswers.answer: Taxes do not keep up with wages, so people pay more. Revenue from profits changes a lot, which makes budgets hard.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies two reasons with limited explanation. The first is not explained accurately, since the issue is unindexed thresholds rather than taxes failing to keep pace with wages.

sampleAnswers.answer: The tax system should be changed because it is old.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Makes a general statement about the tax system without identifying a reason linked to the scenario.

prompts.question: Discuss the case for and against shifting the tax mix from income tax towards consumption taxes as part of reform of the Australian taxation system.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A review panel proposes that the Australian taxation system raise a larger share of its revenue from a broad consumption tax and a smaller share from personal income tax. Supporters argue that the change would reduce disincentives to work and save, while critics argue that consumption taxes fall more heavily on low-income households.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Discusses the case for and against shifting the tax mix, weighing efficiency and equity and reaching a reasoned view on the trade-off that is supported by the scenario
5 marks: Discusses both the case for and the case against with accurate reference to efficiency and equity
4 marks: Discusses one side of the argument with accurate reasoning and some reference to the other
3 marks: Explains one effect of a consumption tax or an income tax with some accuracy
2 marks: Describes income tax or consumption tax with limited accuracy
1 mark: Makes a general statement about taxation reform
markerNotes: Strong answers present both sides and tie the arguments to efficiency and equity, rather than giving an opinion alone
Reward recognition that a consumption tax does not tax saving directly, which is the basis of the efficiency argument
commonStudentErrors: Stating that consumption taxes are fairer than income taxes without reference to equity
Discussing only the case for the change

sampleAnswers.answer: The case for shifting the tax mix rests mainly on efficiency. A personal income tax reduces the return to working and saving, so people may supply less labour and save less than they otherwise would. A broad consumption tax is levied on spending, so it does not penalise saving directly, and a wide base can raise revenue at lower rates. Supporters also argue that consumption taxes are simple to collect, since they are charged at each sale. The case against rests mainly on equity. Consumption taxes are regressive, because low-income households spend a larger share of their income, so the burden falls more heavily on them relative to income. Exemptions to protect these households narrow the base and require higher rates, which weakens the efficiency gain. Reform should therefore weigh the efficiency gains against the equity costs, and may need compensating transfers to protect low-income households.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Presents the case for and against with accurate reasoning on efficiency and equity and reaches a reasoned view on the trade-off. The point about exemptions shows the link between the two sides.

sampleAnswers.answer: Shifting towards consumption taxes could reduce the disincentive to save, so it may be more efficient. However, these taxes are regressive, because poorer households spend more of their income, so it may be unfair.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Discusses both sides briefly with accurate reasoning, but the answer is underdeveloped and the view on the trade-off is not reached.

sampleAnswers.answer: Income tax discourages work. Consumption tax is fairer for everyone.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes one effect of income tax, but the claim that consumption tax is fairer for everyone is inaccurate and is not supported by any reasoning on equity.

dotPoints.description: Purpose of recurrent and non-recurrent government spending, including transfer payments, essential services and infrastructure

prompts.question: Explain the difference between recurrent and non-recurrent government spending, using the two items in the scenario as examples.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A state government's budget provides $40 million a year for the salaries of teachers and nurses, and $300 million, spent over three years, to build a new rail line.
prompts.markingCriteria:
3 marks: Explains the difference between recurrent and non-recurrent government spending, with accurate examples drawn from the scenario
2 marks: Describes recurrent or non-recurrent government spending with an accurate example
1 mark: Identifies recurrent or non-recurrent spending without explanation
markerNotes: Strong answers explain the difference in terms of whether spending repeats each year and what it produces, such as a service or an asset
Reward correct examples that match each type to the scenario item
commonStudentErrors: Describing both types as spending on public services
Classifying the rail line as recurrent because it is paid for over several years

sampleAnswers.answer: Recurrent government spending is ongoing expenditure that is repeated each year, such as the salaries of teachers and nurses in the scenario, which fund the continuing provision of services. Non-recurrent government spending is one-off or capital expenditure that is not repeated, such as the cost of building the rail line, which is infrastructure. Non-recurrent spending creates assets that last for many years, while recurrent spending pays for services as they are delivered.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Explains the difference clearly, using the scenario items correctly and noting what each type produces.

sampleAnswers.answer: Recurrent spending is paid every year, like teachers' salaries. Non-recurrent spending is the rail line.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Describes both types with an accurate example, but the difference is not explained.

sampleAnswers.answer: Recurrent spending is ongoing, and the rail line is one-off.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Identifies the difference in brief terms without explanation.

prompts.question: Analyse the purposes of transfer payments and infrastructure spending in achieving government objectives of income support and economic growth.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A federal government must choose between increasing its recurrent spending on transfer payments, such as an unemployment benefit for people out of work, and increasing its non-recurrent spending on a national road network. Its advisers are concerned about both the living standards of low-income households and the productive capacity of the economy.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Analyses the distinct purposes of transfer payments and infrastructure spending, linking income support to living standards and short-term stabilisation, and infrastructure to long-run productive capacity and economic growth, with a reasoned view on their trade-off
5 marks: Analyses the purposes of both types of spending with accurate reference to income support and economic growth
4 marks: Explains how transfer payments or infrastructure spending meets one government objective with some accuracy
3 marks: Describes transfer payments or infrastructure spending with some relevant detail
2 marks: Identifies one type of government spending with limited explanation
1 mark: Makes a general statement about government objectives
markerNotes: Strong answers separate the short-term purpose of transfers from the long-run effect of infrastructure, rather than treating both as growth spending
Reward a reasoned view on the trade-off that acknowledges timing
commonStudentErrors: Stating that transfer payments increase productive capacity
Describing the two types of spending without linking them to government objectives

sampleAnswers.answer: Transfer payments are recurrent payments made to people without a good or service in return, such as an unemployment benefit.
