sampleAnswers.answer: The same cut has different effects in the two regions, because each economy is exposed to the cash rate through different channels. In Region A, most households have variable-rate mortgages, so the cut lowers their repayments and increases their disposable income. This adds to demand in the city, and because house prices are already rising, it may push asset prices further up and add to financial risk. In Region B, the main channel is the exchange rate. A lower cash rate tends to reduce the value of the Australian dollar, which makes the processed food exported by the town cheaper overseas, so export earnings may rise. The contrast shows that a single national rate cannot target specific areas of the economy. The cut may add to pressure in Region A while supporting Region B, and the Reserve Bank must accept that its tool cannot target either region alone.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: the answer contrasts the household channel in the city with the exchange rate channel in the regional town, uses the scenario facts, and concludes that a single rate cannot target either region.

sampleAnswers.answer: In the city, lower mortgage payments mean households have more to spend, so demand rises. In the regional town, the cut helps exporters because the dollar falls. The national rate affects both places, so it cannot be set separately for each region.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The effect on both regions is described with accurate direction, which earns 3 marks. Contrast the channels explicitly and link them to the scenario facts, such as mortgage type and export dependence, to reach 4 or 5 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: A cash rate cut makes borrowing cheaper, which helps some people more than others.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A general statement earns 2 marks. Apply the cut to Region A and Region B separately, and name the channel that works in each.

dotPoints.description: Role and nature of microeconomic policies, including raising productivity and improving outcomes on social issues to enhance quality of life

prompts.question: Describe the role and nature of microeconomic policies, including raising productivity and improving outcomes on social issues to enhance quality of life.
markerNotes: Reward the distinction that microeconomic policy targets specific markets and the supply side, while macroeconomic policy targets aggregates
Reference to improving productivity as the main source of long-run growth shows understanding of the role
commonStudentErrors: Describing microeconomic policy as the same as macroeconomic policy
Omitting social outcomes such as health and housing
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Describes the role and nature of microeconomic policies accurately, distinguishing them from macroeconomic policy, and explaining their focus on productivity and social outcomes, with examples
3 marks: Describes the nature of microeconomic policy and one of its roles with accurate detail
2 marks: Identifies microeconomic policies with some accuracy
1 mark: Makes a general statement about economic policy

sampleAnswers.answer: Microeconomic policies target specific markets, industries and households rather than total demand. Their main role is to raise productivity, the main long-run driver of living standards. They work on the supply side, by changing competition, regulation, infrastructure and taxation so that resources are used more efficiently. They also address social issues, such as access to health care and housing, which affect quality of life. Macroeconomic policy, such as a change in the cash rate, is directed at aggregate demand across the whole economy. In the scenario, the business-setup reform affects many industries, while the licensing change affects one profession.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: the answer describes the role and nature of microeconomic policy, links productivity and social outcomes to it, and distinguishes it clearly from macroeconomic policy and the cash rate.

sampleAnswers.answer: Microeconomic policies target particular markets and industries. They aim to raise productivity, which helps the economy grow over time.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The answer describes the market focus and the productivity role accurately, which earns 2 marks. Add the social outcomes, and contrast the policy with macroeconomic tools such as the cash rate, to reach 4 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Microeconomic policies affect parts of the economy rather than all of it.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A general statement earns 1 mark. Name the markets targeted and the aim of raising productivity to show the role of microeconomic policy.

prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A government announces two reforms. One lowers the cost of setting up a new business in every industry. Another changes the licensing rules for a single profession. A student is asked to describe what these reforms are designed to do and how they differ from a change in the cash rate.

prompts.question: Classify each of the two packages in the scenario as microeconomic or macroeconomic, and give one reason for each classification.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: The government is considering two packages in the coming budget. The first is a broad income tax cut for all taxpayers, intended to boost household spending across the economy. The second removes a licensing rule that restricts entry to the plumbing trade in one state, with the aim of lowering prices and increasing the number of trades available there.
prompts.markingCriteria:
2 marks: Classifies both packages correctly, each with a reason linked to its target, aggregate demand for the tax cut and a specific market for the licensing change
1 mark: Classifies one package correctly, or classifies both without reasons
markerNotes: Reward the reason that the income tax cut targets total household spending, which makes it macroeconomic, while the licensing change targets one market, which makes it microeconomic

commonStudentErrors: Classifying all tax changes as macroeconomic without considering their target
Classifying the licensing change as macroeconomic because it affects the economy

sampleAnswers.answer: The income tax cut is macroeconomic policy, as it changes aggregate demand across the economy. The licensing rule change is microeconomic policy because it targets one specific market, aiming to lower prices and raise productivity by easing entry.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: both packages are classified correctly, and each classification is justified by its target, aggregate demand for the tax cut and a specific market for the licensing change.

dotPoints.description: Microeconomic reform to improve productivity in Australia in the areas of competition policy, regulation and deregulation, infrastructure development and taxation

prompts.question: Explain microeconomic reform to improve productivity in Australia in the areas of competition policy, regulation and deregulation, infrastructure development and taxation.
markerNotes: Reward the explanation that competition policy disciplines firms, which lowers prices and encourages efficiency, and that the ACCC enforces it
Linking tax reform to the incentives for investment and work shows analysis of the mechanism
commonStudentErrors: Describing reforms without explaining how they raise productivity
Confusing deregulation with the removal of all rules
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Explains clearly microeconomic reform to improve productivity in competition policy, regulation and deregulation, infrastructure and taxation, with the mechanism by which each raises productivity and a precise example
5 marks: Explains at least three areas of reform with accurate mechanisms and examples

3 marks: Describes microeconomic reform with some accuracy

1 mark: Makes a general statement about reform

sampleAnswers.answer: Microeconomic reform raises productivity by improving how markets and firms operate. Competition policy, enforced by the ACCC under the Competition and Consumer Act 2010, prevents firms from abusing market power. When firms face effective rivals, they must cut costs, improve products and adopt better technology, which lifts productivity across the economy. Regulation and deregulation work through compliance costs and barriers to entry. Simplifying rules, such as the planning approvals for a new industrial estate, lowers the cost of doing business and allows new firms to enter markets, while essential standards must still be protected. Infrastructure development raises productivity by reducing the time and cost of moving goods. Better roads and rail allow freight firms to reach markets more quickly and at lower cost. Taxation reform, such as lowering business tax settings, improves productivity by reducing taxes that discourage investment, which encourages firms to expand. Each reform works by lowering costs or improving incentives, so the economy produces more output from the same inputs.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: each reform is explained with its mechanism for raising productivity, real institutions are named accurately, and the answer shows how each reform lowers costs or improves incentives.

sampleAnswers.answer: Competition policy stops firms from acting unfairly, which encourages efficiency. Reducing regulation lowers costs for businesses. Better roads and rail cut transport costs for freight, which helps productivity.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Each reform is linked to productivity with some accuracy, which earns 3 marks. Explain the mechanism in more detail for each reform, and link them to the freight sector in the scenario, to reach 5 or 6 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Reform helps the economy become more productive.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A general statement earns 1 mark. Name a specific reform and explain how it changes costs or incentives in a market.

prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A state government considers reforming planning approvals for a new industrial estate. A federal review examines whether competition rules, road and rail investment and business tax settings are limiting productivity in the freight sector.

prompts.question: Propose one microeconomic reform that would raise productivity in the freight sector described in the scenario, showing how it would work.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: Freight trucks in a regional area take an average of three hours longer than necessary to move goods to port, because of a single rail crossing that causes long waits and slow approval processes for new depots. Local firms report that transport costs are a large part of their input costs.
prompts.markingCriteria:
4 marks: Proposes a specific, feasible microeconomic reform that targets the bottleneck or approval delays, and shows clearly how it would reduce time or cost and raise productivity in the freight sector
3 marks: Proposes a reform linked to the scenario and explains one way it would raise productivity
2 marks: Proposes a reform with a general link to productivity, without using the scenario
1 mark: States that the government should improve the freight sector
markerNotes: Reward a proposal that targets the stated bottleneck directly, such as a grade separation at the rail crossing or a fixed timeline for depot approvals, and explains the time saved
Strong answers identify the likely trade-off, such as the cost of the project or the need for coordination between levels of government
commonStudentErrors: Proposing a macroeconomic measure, such as a cut in the cash rate, for a supply-side problem
Proposing a reform without explaining how it raises productivity

sampleAnswers.answer: A targeted microeconomic reform would separate the rail crossing from road traffic through infrastructure development, such as a grade separation, and set a fixed timeline for depot approvals. The rail crossing is the main source of delay, so removing the conflict between trains and trucks would let freight move without waiting. Simpler regulation of approval processes for new depots, with a statutory timeframe, would reduce the uncertainty that firms face when they need more capacity. Both changes raise productivity by letting the same trucks, drivers and depots produce more, and less time per delivery lowers transport costs for local firms. The main trade-off is the cost of the project and the need for state and local governments to coordinate.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: the reform targets the rail crossing and the approval delays named in the scenario, the mechanism for raising productivity is explained, and the cost trade-off is recognised.

sampleAnswers.answer: The government could build a new road to speed up freight, which would help productivity in the region.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The proposal is linked to productivity in general, but it does not target the bottleneck named in the scenario, so it earns 2 marks. Propose a reform aimed at the rail crossing or the approval delays, and explain the time saved, to reach 3 or 4 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: The government should improve the freight sector.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A general statement earns 1 mark. Name a specific reform and explain how it reduces delay or cost in the freight sector.

dotPoints.description: Microeconomic policies to reduce inequality and improve wellbeing in the areas of health and housing in Australia

prompts.question: Analyse microeconomic policies to reduce inequality and improve wellbeing in the areas of health and housing in Australia.
markerNotes: Strong answers recognise that subsidies for health care and social housing address access for low-income households, while supply policies address affordability
Reward reference to Medicare and to social and community housing as precise policy examples
commonStudentErrors: Describing policies without linking them to inequality
Treating health and housing as separate from wellbeing
prompts.markingCriteria:
7-8 marks: Makes a sustained analysis of microeconomic policies to reduce inequality and improve wellbeing in health and housing, weighing their effect on access and outcomes for different groups, with a reasoned conclusion on their effectiveness
5-6 marks: Analyses policies in both health and housing with accurate examples and a link to inequality
3-4 marks: Describes health and housing policies with some accuracy
1-2 marks: Makes a basic or general statement about social policy

sampleAnswers.answer: Microeconomic policies in health and housing aim to reduce inequality and improve wellbeing by widening access and improving outcomes for disadvantaged households. In health, Medicare provides universal access to doctors and hospitals, and bulk-billing removes out-of-pocket costs for many visits, which lowers a major barrier for low-income households. The Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme limits the cost of medicines, which helps people with chronic conditions stay in treatment. Bulk-billing rates have varied over time and across regions, so the effect of Medicare depends on local GP availability. However, access is not uniform, because waiting times and the availability of services in regional areas vary, so the policy may narrow the gap in cost without fully closing the gap in access. Public housing waiting lists in many states are long, which limits how far social housing alone can close the gap. In housing, social housing provided by state governments and community housing providers offers rents below the market for eligible households, which directly lowers housing costs. Commonwealth Rent Assistance supports renters on low incomes, but it can push up rents if the supply of housing is limited, so part of the benefit may flow to landlords. Rent assistance is paid to tenants in the private market, so its value depends on the rents charged, which is why it must be considered alongside housing supply. Supply-side policies, such as planning reform that allows more homes to be built, address the cause of unaffordability and may have more lasting effects, although they take longer to work. Negative gearing and the capital gains tax discount for investors can increase demand for rental properties, which may raise prices and work against affordability. The distributional effect also depends on how the policies are funded, because subsidies paid from general revenue are financed by all taxpayers, including the low-income households that receive them. Overall, these policies reduce inequality most effectively when they widen access for low-income households and increase housing supply together, rather than relying on subsidies to demand alone.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: each health and housing policy is linked to its effect on access and wellbeing, the trade-offs and limits of demand-side subsidies are weighed, and the answer reaches a reasoned conclusion about inequality.

sampleAnswers.answer: Medicare provides universal access to health services, and bulk-billing reduces the out-of-pocket cost of visits for low-income households. Social housing gives affordable rent to households on low incomes. However, rent assistance may push up rents if the supply of housing is limited, so the effect on inequality is not certain. The overall effect depends on the mix of policies.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Two policies are linked to low-income households with accurate reference, which places the answer in the 5-6 band. Weigh the limits of demand-side subsidies and the role of housing supply to reach 7-8 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Governments provide health care and housing support to help poorer households.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A brief statement earns 2 marks at most. Name a specific policy, such as Medicare or social housing, and explain how it changes access for low-income households.

prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A city has a shortage of affordable rental housing, and a large share of low-income households spend a high proportion of their income on rent. The government is considering whether to expand social housing and increase rent assistance, and whether to expand access to public health care for low-income residents.

prompts.question: Examine how microeconomic policies in health and housing affect the wellbeing of low-income and high-income households differently.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: Two households live in the same city. Household X earns $45,000 a year, rents its home and has a chronic condition that requires regular medication. Household Y earns $180,000 a year, owns its home with a mortgage and holds private hospital cover.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Examines clearly how the different effects on the two households, explaining how Medicare and the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme lower costs for Household X and Commonwealth Rent Assistance supports its rent, while the private health insurance rebate mainly benefits households able to afford private cover, and weighs the net effect on inequality and wellbeing
5 marks: Examines the different effects of at least two policies on both households, with accurate reference to the scenario
4 marks: Examines the effect of one health or housing policy on one household, with accurate reference to the scenario
3 marks: Describes health and housing policies and their general effect on households
2 marks: Identifies a health or housing policy without explaining its effect
1 mark: States that policies affect different households
markerNotes: Reward accurate use of named policies, such as Medicare, the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme, Commonwealth Rent Assistance and the private health insurance rebate
Strong answers weigh whether a policy reduces inequality in access or mainly benefits households that already have more income
commonStudentErrors: Describing health and housing policies without relating them to the two households
Assuming that every policy reduces inequality for low-income households

sampleAnswers.answer: Microeconomic policies affect the two households differently, because each reaches them through a different cost and eligibility route. For Household X, Medicare gives access to doctors and hospitals, and bulk-billing reduces the out-of-pocket cost of many visits, which matters on $45,000 a year. The Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme limits the cost of regular medication, so the chronic condition is less of a financial burden. Commonwealth Rent Assistance helps Household X meet part of its rent, which supports its wellbeing. These policies reduce inequality in access, because they lower the cost barriers that would otherwise prevent Household X from receiving care and housing support. For Household Y, which can already afford private hospital cover, the private health insurance rebate lowers the cost of that cover. The rebate does little for Household X, so it adds to the support of the higher-income household rather than reducing inequality. Household Y gains little from rent assistance, as it owns its home. On balance, the policies narrow the gap in wellbeing, but how far they reduce inequality depends on their scale and on the quality of public services available to Household X.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: the answer accounts for each policy's effect on each household, names the policies accurately, and weighs whether the net effect reduces inequality in access and wellbeing.

sampleAnswers.answer: Medicare gives Household X access to doctors, and bulk-billing reduces the cost of visits. Commonwealth Rent Assistance helps Household X meet its rent. The private health insurance rebate mainly reduces the cost of cover for households that can already afford it, such as Household Y, so it does little for Household X.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Two policies are examined with accurate reference to both households, which places the answer in the 5 band. Weigh the overall effect on inequality and wellbeing, and explain the housing effect for Household Y, to reach the full 6 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Medicare helps people see a doctor, and rent help assists renters.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The policies are identified but their effects on the households are not explained, which earns 2 marks. Explain how each policy changes the cost of care or housing for Household X and Household Y.

dotPoints.description: Effects of microeconomic policies on households, businesses, the government and the economy

prompts.question: Analyse the effects of microeconomic policies on households, businesses, the government and the economy.
markerNotes: Strong answers show that competition reform benefits consumers but can impose adjustment costs on incumbent firms
Reward recognition that the government may lose revenue from tax reform in the short run, with gains later
commonStudentErrors: Describing effects on one group only
Assuming all policies benefit all groups equally
prompts.markingCriteria:
7-8 marks: Makes a sustained analysis of the effects of microeconomic policies on households, businesses, the government and the economy, weighing the gains and costs for each group and reaching a reasoned judgement
5-6 marks: Analyses the effects on at least three of these groups with accurate examples
3-4 marks: Describes effects of microeconomic policies with some accuracy
1-2 marks: Makes a basic or general statement about policy effects

sampleAnswers.answer: The effects of microeconomic policies fall on households, businesses, the government and the economy in different ways. Households that use the buses may gain most directly, because fares on the routes fall by 10 per cent and services become more frequent, which lowers the cost of getting to work, school and services. However, the gains are not certain for every household, because new operators may not serve less profitable routes, so some outer suburbs could lose service. Businesses are affected unevenly. New operators gain access to a market and can earn profits by competing on price and service, but the two incumbent operators face lower profits, and their workers may face adjustment costs if the firms reduce staff or routes. The government's position improves in one respect, because annual subsidy payments fall by $20 million, which frees budget resources for other services. The government must also carry costs, such as regulating routes, monitoring service standards and managing contracts, and these costs may offset part of the saving. For the economy, competition may improve efficiency and lower transport costs for other industries that rely on buses to move workers, which supports productivity over time. The effect on the government is also a matter of contracts, since the state must decide how much subsidy to pay for routes that new operators choose not to serve. Households on lower incomes, who rely on buses most, are likely to benefit from lower fares, which may make the distribution of the gains more favourable than the aggregate figures suggest. The net assessment depends on whether service standards are maintained on all routes, because the gains for regular users and the budget saving can be undermined if coverage falls for people who depend on the service most. Overall, the reform is likely to produce net gains for most users and the budget, but its design, particularly route obligations, determines whether the benefits are shared fairly.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: the answer analyses the effects on households, incumbent and new firms, the budget and the economy, weighs the gains against the costs and the risk to outer routes, and reaches a reasoned conclusion.

sampleAnswers.answer: Households that use the buses gain, because fares on the routes fall by 10 per cent and services become more frequent. Incumbent operators lose profits because they now face new rivals. The state saves $20 million a year in subsidy payments. However, some routes may lose service if new operators do not find them profitable, so the gains are not shared equally across the community.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The effects on users, incumbents and the budget are analysed with accurate reference to the scenario, which places the answer in the 5-6 band. Weigh the costs of regulation and the effect on less profitable routes to reach 7-8 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Competition makes bus fares lower, which helps households.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A brief statement earns 2 marks. Analyse the effect on at least two groups, using the scenario figures, to move up the ladder.

prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A state government reforms a city bus service by allowing new private operators to compete for routes. Within a year, fares on the routes fall by 10 per cent and bus frequency rises, but two incumbent operators report lower profits, and the state's annual subsidy payments to the service fall by $20 million.

prompts.question: Deduce, from the data in the scenario, the likely effects of the reform on households, incumbent firms and the government's budget.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: After a competition reform in the coastal freight market, the average price of freight falls by 8 per cent, the number of firms rises from 5 to 8, and the profit margins of incumbent firms fall by 4 percentage points. The government's tax revenue from the industry falls by $15 million a year, while its spending on industry support falls by $6 million a year.

5 marks: Deduces clearly from the data that households and freight users gain from lower prices, that incumbent margins fall, and that the budget loses $15 million of revenue but saves $6 million of support, weighing the net budget effect and reaching a reasoned conclusion
4 marks: Deduces the effects on two groups from the data with accurate figures
3 marks: Deduces the effect on one group from the data, with accurate figures
2 marks: Describes the likely effects of the reform without using the data
1 mark: States that the reform affects households and businesses
markerNotes: Reward the deduction that the budget loses $15 million of tax revenue but saves $6 million of support, a net cost of $9 million a year
Strong answers note that the gains to freight users are clear from the price fall, while the effect on incumbents depends on how entry continues

Assuming that incumbent firms gain from more competition

sampleAnswers.answer: The effects of the competition reform are uneven across the groups in the scenario. Households and freight users gain most directly, because the average price of freight falls by 8 per cent, which lowers the cost of the goods they buy. The effect on incumbent firms is negative: their profit margins fall by 4 percentage points, even though the number of competitors has risen from five to eight. For the government budget, the effect is a net cost. Tax revenue from the industry falls by $15 million a year, while spending on industry support falls by $6 million a year, so the net effect is a reduction of $9 million a year. The conclusion is that the reform most likely benefits freight users and costs the budget about $9 million a year, although the size of the wider gain depends on whether new firms continue to enter the market.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: the answer deduces each group's effect from the scenario figures, including the net $9 million budget cost, and reaches a conclusion that states what the outcome depends on.

sampleAnswers.answer: Freight prices fall by 8 per cent, so households and businesses that use freight gain. The number of firms rises, which may be good for competition. The government's budget loses $15 million of tax revenue each year.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The price and revenue effects are deduced with accurate figures for one group each, which earns 3 marks. Use the margin fall for incumbents and the net budget effect, and weigh them together, to reach 4 or 5 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: The reform helps households and hurts incumbent firms.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A general statement earns 1 mark. Deduce the effect on households, incumbents and the budget from the specific figures.

dotPoints.description: Effectiveness of microeconomic policies in achieving Australia’s economic objectives

prompts.question: Assess the effectiveness of microeconomic policies in achieving Australia’s economic objectives.
markerNotes: Strong answers recognise that microeconomic reform has large but slow effects, and that its effectiveness is harder to measure than fiscal or monetary effects
Reward evidence from productivity data or from reform evaluations to support the judgement
commonStudentErrors: Assessing effectiveness without evidence
Treating reform as immediately effective
prompts.markingCriteria:
7-8 marks: Makes a sustained, criteria-based assessment of the effectiveness of microeconomic policies in achieving Australia's economic objectives, weighing the effects on productivity, growth and living standards, the lags, the distribution of gains and the strength of the evidence, and reaching a supported judgement
5-6 marks: Assesses the effectiveness of microeconomic policies with accurate evidence on productivity or prices, and some consideration of lags or distribution
4 marks: Describes the effects of microeconomic reforms on productivity or prices, with some reference to evidence
2-3 marks: Makes a basic statement about the effect of microeconomic reform on the economy
1 mark: Makes a general statement that reforms are meant to improve the economy

sampleAnswers.answer: The effectiveness of microeconomic policies is credible in principle, because they lower costs, improve incentives and encourage firms to use resources more efficiently. The review's findings suggest that they have worked in part. Prices fell in some sectors, which benefits households directly, and productivity growth was slightly higher than before the package. Productivity matters because it underpins growth in living standards over the long run, and Australia's productivity growth has slowed compared with earlier decades, so even modest gains are significant. However, the evidence is limited in size. A slight increase in productivity growth is a small improvement, and it is hard to isolate the effects of the package from other influences, such as technological change and global conditions. The lags are also long. Competition and regulatory reforms can change firm behaviour within a few years, but infrastructure investment often takes longer to show in productivity, so an assessment after three years may understate its eventual effect. The distribution of gains is a further limit. The review finds that gains varied widely between regions, which suggests that the package improved efficiency in some areas more than others, and a policy that leaves some regions behind is less effective against Australia's economic objectives, which include prosperity for all Australians. The judgement also depends on the counterfactual. If productivity would have grown at a similar rate without the package, the reforms would have had little effect, and the review would need data from comparable periods or regions to establish how much of the change the package caused. Lower prices in some sectors help households on fixed incomes, but the benefit is smaller where competition has not been introduced. Overall, the reforms appear to have been moderately effective, because they lowered some prices and helped productivity, but their effect on living standards depends on the size and timing of the productivity gains and on whether regional gains are spread more evenly.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: the answer weighs the productivity and price effects against the lags, the difficulty of isolating the effects and the uneven regional gains, and reaches a supported judgement.

sampleAnswers.answer: Competition reform has supported lower prices in some sectors. Infrastructure investment supports growth, but the review's productivity gain is slight, and the effects of the package varied between regions. Microeconomic reform is effective in principle, but its effect on productivity may take years to appear fully, so a three-year review may understate its benefit.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The answer assesses the price and productivity evidence with some accuracy, and it considers the lags, which places it in the 5-6 band. Weigh the distribution of gains and the strength of the evidence to reach 7-8 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Microeconomic reforms are meant to make the economy more productive.
sampleAnswers.feedback: A basic statement earns 2 marks. Explain the effect of the reforms on prices or productivity, using the scenario, to move up the ladder.

prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A review of a three-year package of competition, regulatory and infrastructure reforms finds that prices fell in some sectors, that productivity growth was slightly higher than before the package, and that the gains varied widely between regions.

prompts.question: Analyse the effectiveness of the competition reform and the infrastructure program in raising productivity, using the figures in the scenario.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A review estimates that a competition reform raised labour productivity growth by 0.3 percentage points a year within two years of its introduction. A $5 billion infrastructure program raised productivity growth by 0.2 percentage points a year, but the effect was only measurable six years after the program began.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Analyses clearly the speed, size and durability of the two effects, using both figures, and reaches a supported judgement on which reform is more effective and under what conditions
5 marks: Analyses the two reforms with accurate reference to both figures, identifying the difference in timing or size
4 marks: Compares the size or timing of the two effects with some accurate reference to the figures
3 marks: Describes the effect of each reform on productivity, with some reference to the scenario
2 marks: Describes one reform's effect on productivity without using the figures
1 mark: States that both reforms affect productivity
markerNotes: Reward the use of both figures: the competition reform adds 0.3 percentage points a year within two years, while the infrastructure program adds 0.2 percentage points after six years

sampleAnswers.answer: The effectiveness of the two microeconomic policies differs over time. The competition reform raised labour productivity growth by 0.3 percentage points a year within two years, so its benefit appears quickly and while the policy is still being implemented. The infrastructure program raised productivity growth by only 0.2 percentage points a year, and that effect was measurable only six years after the program began, which reflects its lags. On the figures alone, the reform is the more effective policy for early productivity growth. However, the size of the effect is not the only measure. Infrastructure investment may be more durable, because roads, rail and digital networks remain in use for decades and continue to lower the cost of moving goods and people, so its gain may accumulate to a larger total. The competition gain depends on entry continuing, which may weaken if markets become concentrated again. If the aim is to reduce prices quickly, the competition reform has the advantage, whereas if the aim is to raise the economy's capacity over decades, the infrastructure program may be the stronger choice. The judgement therefore depends on the time horizon used to evaluate the microeconomic policies, and on whether their benefits are sustained.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: the answer compares the speed and the durability of the two effects using both figures, and reaches a judgement that depends on the time horizon.

sampleAnswers.answer: The competition reform raises productivity growth by 0.3 percentage points within two years, which is faster and larger than the infrastructure program's 0.2 percentage points. The infrastructure effect only appears after six years. So the reform is more effective, at least in the short run.
sampleAnswers.feedback: The timing and size of the two effects are compared accurately, which earns 4 marks. Consider how long each effect lasts and judge the policies over a longer horizon to reach 5 or 6 marks.

dotPoints.description: Limitations to the effectiveness of microeconomic policies, including policy lags, political considerations and regulatory capture

prompts.question: Explain the limitations to the effectiveness of microeconomic policies, including policy lags, political considerations and regulatory capture.
markerNotes: Reward the explanation of regulatory capture, where a regulator comes to serve the interests of the industry it regulates

sampleAnswers.answer: Microeconomic policies face several limitations that reduce their effectiveness. Policy lags are the first: reforms to competition rules or regulation often take years to change firm behaviour and show up in productivity, so a reform may be diluted before its benefits appear. Political considerations are the second. Governments may avoid reforms that impose visible losses on organised groups, even where the total gain is larger, and these considerations are strongest near an election, when losses are concentrated and gains are delayed. Regulatory capture is the third, in which a regulator comes to serve the industry it oversees. In the scenario, the ferry regulator's hiring of former executives of the incumbent operator, together with the operator's lobbying, means the new competition may be weakened, delayed or designed to protect the incumbent. Regulatory capture also has a longer-term cost, because new entrants may decide not to invest in a market where the rules are unlikely to be applied fairly. The combined effect is that a reform can be approved on paper but applied so narrowly that its productivity benefit is small.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: each limitation is explained with its mechanism, the lags and political constraints are explained, and regulatory capture is linked to the ferry route in the scenario.

sampleAnswers.answer: Reforms take years to show results, so the benefits may not appear quickly. Governments may also delay reforms that upset powerful groups. Regulatory capture can happen when a regulator favours the industry it oversees.

sampleAnswers.answer: Microeconomic policies do not always succeed.

sampleAnswers.answer: Wages in Australia are set through three main wage-setting mechanisms. Individual arrangements are agreements between an employer and a single employee, such as individual flexibility arrangements, which may vary award terms, such as hours, only where the employee is better off overall. Enterprise bargaining agreements are negotiated at the enterprise level and must be approved by the Fair Work Commission, which applies the better-off-overall test. Industry awards set minimum conditions, including minimum pay rates, for occupations and industries under the Fair Work Act 2009, and they form the safety net. In the scenario, the factory worker is paid under an enterprise agreement, the aged-care employee under an industry award, and the senior manager under an individual contract.

dotPoints.description: Advantages and disadvantages of centralised and decentralised wage determination

prompts.question: Assess the advantages and disadvantages of centralised and decentralised wage determination.
markerNotes: Strong answers recognise that centralised systems provide consistency and protect low-paid workers, but may not reflect local productivity
Reward recognition that decentralised bargaining can reward productivity but may widen gaps between workers with different bargaining power
commonStudentErrors: Describing the systems without assessing advantages and disadvantages
Treating one system as always superior
prompts.markingCriteria:
7-8 marks: Makes a sustained, criteria-based assessment of the advantages and disadvantages of centralised and decentralised wage determination, weighing their effects on fairness, flexibility, productivity and inflation, and reaching a supported judgement
5-6 marks: Assesses the advantages and disadvantages of both systems with accurate evidence and some weighing of their effects
4 marks: Describes the features and some advantages or disadvantages of centralised and decentralised systems
2-3 marks: Makes a basic statement about one of the two wage systems
1 mark: Makes a general statement that wages are set in different ways

sampleAnswers.answer: The advantages of centralised wage determination, in which wages are set for a whole industry, include consistency and protection for low-paid workers. A single industry-wide agreement gives all support staff the same minimum conditions, which reduces the risk that workers with weak bargaining power are underpaid, and it reduces the cost of negotiating many separate agreements. It also supports fairness by treating similar work similarly across hospitals. The disadvantages are that a single rate cannot reflect differences in local labour markets, productivity or the financial position of individual hospitals. Centralised systems can also reduce flexibility, because changes in conditions take longer to negotiate and may not suit each workplace. Decentralised wage determination, in which each hospital negotiates its own agreement, can reward productivity and allow pay to reflect local conditions, such as the difficulty of recruiting staff in regional areas. It gives managers and staff room to trade conditions for better outcomes. Its disadvantage is that workers with less bargaining power may be left with weaker agreements, which widens gaps between hospitals and between workers. Decentralised bargaining also requires more negotiation, which can increase costs and make it harder to keep standards consistent across the public system. The effect on inflation depends on the outcomes: a centralised agreement may set a pattern that spreads to other sectors, while decentralised bargaining may allow pay to respond more closely to productivity, which supports price stability if pay is not pushed up by competition for staff in one workplace. In the scenario, a single industry agreement would protect support staff who have little bargaining power, but it would not reflect the different conditions of hospitals in regional areas. The judgement depends on the weight given to fairness and consistency compared with flexibility and local productivity, and a hybrid arrangement, with a common minimum and local bargaining above it, may combine the strengths of both systems.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: both systems are assessed on fairness, flexibility, productivity and inflation, the scenario is used to weigh them, and the answer reaches a supported judgement that includes a hybrid option.

sampleAnswers.answer: Centralised wage setting offers consistency and protects low-paid workers, because one agreement covers all support staff. It also reduces the cost of negotiating many separate agreements. However, it may not reflect local conditions, so regional hospitals may find it harder to recruit. Decentralised bargaining can reward productivity at each hospital, but workers with weak bargaining power may get worse outcomes.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Both systems are assessed with accurate points, which places the answer in the 5-6 band. Add the effects on productivity and inflation and weigh them in the scenario, to reach 7-8 marks.

sampleAnswers.answer: Centralised wage determination would improve outcomes for low-paid workers in some respects, but its effect on jobs and productivity means the overall outcome is not clear-cut. The main benefit is protection. In the care industry in the scenario, low-paid workers often have little bargaining power against individual employers, so an industry-wide minimum sets a floor below which pay cannot fall. Consistency is a further benefit, because similar work is paid similarly across employers. The main risk is that a single rate may be set above what some employers can afford, particularly in lower-productivity regional firms, which could reduce hours or employment for the workers the policy is meant to protect. Centralised systems also struggle to reflect local productivity, which is why employers argue that pay should match what each business can afford. A common minimum set with regard to employment effects, with local bargaining above it, would protect low-paid workers while keeping some flexibility. On balance, centralised determination would improve outcomes for the lowest-paid workers only if the rate is set carefully.

dotPoints.description: Costs and benefits of non-standard work arrangements for individuals, businesses and the economy

prompts.question: Analyse the costs and benefits of non-standard work arrangements for individuals, businesses and the economy.
markerNotes: Strong answers recognise that flexibility benefits some workers, such as students and carers, while others face income insecurity
Reward the observation that businesses gain flexibility but may face higher turnover and lower investment in training
commonStudentErrors: Describing only the costs or only the benefits
Treating non-standard work as uniform
prompts.markingCriteria:
7-8 marks: Makes a sustained analysis of the costs and benefits of non-standard work arrangements for individuals, businesses and the economy, weighing flexibility against insecurity, with a reasoned conclusion
5-6 marks: Analyses the costs and benefits for at least two of these groups with accurate examples
3-4 marks: Describes non-standard work arrangements with some accuracy

sampleAnswers.answer: Non-standard work arrangements, including casual, part-time and contract work, have costs and benefits for individuals, businesses and the economy, and the balance depends on whether workers have protections. For individuals, the main benefit is flexibility. Students and carers can fit work around study and family responsibilities, and some workers enter the labour market who would otherwise find it hard to do so. The costs are income insecurity, because casual hours can change at short notice, and fewer paid entitlements. Casual employees receive a loading in place of paid leave, but they cannot rely on that income in the same way as a permanent worker. Independent contractors have fewer minimum entitlements, so the delivery drivers in the scenario carry more of the risk of low or uncertain earnings. For businesses, casual and contract work allows labour to be matched to demand, which reduces fixed costs and helps manage peak periods. The costs are lower commitment from workers, higher turnover, and less investment in training, which can reduce productivity over time. Businesses also face legal risk if contractor arrangements are not genuine, because sham contracting is prohibited under the Fair Work Act 2009. For the economy, non-standard work can raise employment participation and make it easier for firms to adjust to changes in demand. However, insecure income may lead households to save more and spend less, which weakens demand, and it may widen inequality if the benefits go mainly to employers and workers who choose flexibility. Non-standard work also affects the business's own training and retention decisions, since workers who expect short tenure have less reason to invest in skills. The scenario shows both sides. Casual roles offer flexibility to some staff but unpredictable income for others, and contractor arrangements shift risk to drivers. The net benefit is therefore positive when the arrangements are chosen freely and workers have access to minimum protections, and it becomes negative when they are used to avoid those protections.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: costs and benefits are analysed for individuals, businesses and the economy, the risk shifted to contractors is weighed against the flexibility gained, and the answer reaches a reasoned judgement about when the net benefit holds.

sampleAnswers.answer: Casual and part-time work gives flexibility to students and carers, and businesses can match staff to demand. However, casual workers have less income security, and they do not receive paid leave, although a loading is paid in its place. Independent contractors may not receive minimum entitlements, so the platform shifts some risk onto drivers. The overall effect depends on how many workers choose these arrangements.

The key assumption of any extrapolation is that the pattern in the data continues unchanged, and this limits the reliability of the estimate. A recession, a change in the rules on casual work, or a shift in demand for flexible labour could slow or reverse the trend. Because the trend rests on only three observations, the estimate is also sensitive to small changes in the data. Even if the trend continues, a rising casual share has implications for income security, because casual workers generally have less certain hours and income and fewer paid entitlements than permanent employees. The extrapolation therefore points to a substantial share of insecure work by 2035 if no policy changes occur.

dotPoints.description: Purpose of the industrial safety net, including the minimum wage

prompts.question: Explain the purpose of the industrial safety net, including the minimum wage.

sampleAnswers.answer: The industrial safety net is a set of minimum standards that apply to all employees, regardless of how their pay is set. Its purpose is to protect workers who have weak bargaining power, such as young or part-time workers, so that an employer cannot push pay and conditions below a basic level. The safety net has three main parts. The National Employment Standards set ten minimum entitlements, including annual leave and parental leave. Modern awards set minimum pay rates and conditions for occupations and industries, and the national minimum wage is set each year by the Fair Work Commission. In the scenario, the employer's proposal to pay below the award rate is not permitted, because an employer cannot offer pay below the minimum set by the award, even with the worker's agreement to share profits. Profit sharing could supplement the award, but it cannot replace the minimum. Together, these elements give workers a floor of pay and conditions that does not depend on individual bargaining skill.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: the purpose of the safety net is explained, its three parts are named accurately, and the answer applies the protection to the scenario in which pay below the award is not permitted.

dotPoints.description: Effects of changes in union representation on bargaining power and wages in Australia

prompts.question: Explain the effects of changes in union representation on bargaining power and wages in Australia.

sampleAnswers.answer: Union representation affects bargaining power because unions negotiate collectively, which gives workers more leverage than they have as individuals. A union can credibly threaten industrial action, and high membership means more workers are covered by collective agreements, so employers are more likely to offer pay above the minimum to avoid disputes. Falling membership reduces this leverage. In the scenario, fewer workers are covered, and new hires are offered individual arrangements on terms that reflect their weaker individual bargaining position. Lower coverage tends to slow wage growth, particularly for low-paid workers, because the weaker bargaining position reduces the pressure on employers to share productivity gains. The decentralisation of bargaining, through individual arrangements, adds to this effect, because workers with less information and less bargaining power may accept smaller increases. As bargaining power shifts towards employers, a larger share of income may go to profits rather than wages, although technological change also affects the wage share. Overall, the decline in union representation is likely to reduce the bargaining power of workers in the town and slow wage growth for many of them.
sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: the answer links falling membership to weaker bargaining power, explains how this slows wage growth through coverage and individual arrangements, and recognises other influences on the wage share.

sampleAnswers.answer: Unions negotiate collectively, so workers have more bargaining power than individuals. When union membership falls, fewer workers are covered by agreements, so employers have more power to set pay. This can slow wage growth in the town.

dotPoints.description: Role of education and training funding and migration policy to improve the size and skills of the Australian workforce

prompts.question: Explain the role of education and training funding and migration policy in improving the size and skills of the Australian workforce.
markerNotes: Reward the distinction that training improves skills and productivity, while migration increases the size of the workforce
Recognising the trade-off between skilled migration and the training of domestic workers shows evaluation
commonStudentErrors: Describing education and migration without linking them to the workforce
Ignoring the difference between size and skills
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Explains clearly how education and training funding and migration policy improve the size and skills of the Australian workforce, with precise examples such as vocational training and skilled migration programs and the trade-offs involved
5 marks: Explains both education and training and migration policy with accurate examples
4 marks: Explains one of these policies with accurate detail
3 marks: Describes workforce policies with some accuracy
2 marks: Identifies a training or migration policy
1 mark: Makes a general statement about workforce development

sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: the answer explains how training and migration each affect the size and the skills of the workforce, uses precise examples, and identifies the trade-off in timing between the two policies.
sampleAnswers.answer: Education and training funding raises workforce skills by improving the productivity of existing workers. Government subsidies for vocational training, delivered through TAFE institutes and registered training organisations, lower the cost of gaining a qualification, so more people complete courses in trades and health care. Higher skill levels increase productivity, which raises wages and keeps workers employed as industries change. Migration policy affects workforce size directly. Skilled migration visas bring in workers who fill vacancies in occupations where local supply is short, increasing the number of people employed and the output the economy can produce. Migrants also bring skills that local workers may lack. Education funding and migration are complementary: training builds the domestic pipeline over several years, while migration fills immediate gaps. Funding can also target under-represented groups, such as young people and people returning after long absences, which widens the pool of skilled workers. Migration policy can be adjusted quickly, which makes it useful when a specific shortage is urgent, although it must be balanced against housing and infrastructure pressures. Both policies therefore improve workforce size and skills, although the benefits of training take longer to appear than those of migration.

sampleAnswers.feedback: A 3-mark response describes the policies with some accuracy but does not explain how each changes the size or the skills of the workforce in a linked way, and gives no precise example of a program.
sampleAnswers.answer: Training funding gives workers skills, which can make them more productive. Migration also helps because skilled migrants can fill jobs that employers cannot fill locally. The answer does not explain how these policies change the size of the workforce overall.

sampleAnswers.feedback: A 1-mark response makes a general statement about workforce development and does not identify a policy.
sampleAnswers.answer: Education and migration are important for the workforce.

prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A national review finds that the workforce is growing more slowly than planned and that many new workers lack the technical and digital skills employers need. The review considers funding more vocational education and training places, and it also considers changing the number of skilled migration places available each year.

prompts.question: Discuss the trade-offs between funding education and training and expanding migration as responses to a skills shortage in a hypothetical regional economy.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A regional economy has persistent vacancies for electricians, aged-care workers and engineers that local employers say they cannot fill. The state government can increase funding for vocational education and training, and the federal government can increase the number of skilled migration visas for these occupations. Both options cost money and take different lengths of time to affect the workforce.
prompts.markingCriteria:
7-8 marks: Makes a sustained discussion of the trade-offs between training funding and migration for the hypothetical skills shortage, weighing speed, cost, the durability of skills and effects on local workers, and reaches a reasoned view on how the two policies should be balanced
5-6 marks: Discusses the trade-offs between the two policies with accurate reasoning about timing and cost and at least one further effect
4 marks: Discusses one policy and its trade-offs with accurate detail
2-3 marks: Describes education and migration policy with limited discussion of the trade-offs
1 mark: Makes a minimal relevant statement
markerNotes: Reward the point that training takes years to produce qualified workers while migration can fill vacancies within months, so the two options trade speed against durability
A discussion must weigh the options against each other and reach a view on the balance, not describe each policy separately
commonStudentErrors: Describing both policies without weighing one against the other
Ignoring the time lag between training investment and workforce outcomes
Treating migration as costless for local workers without considering effects on local wages

sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: the answer weighs speed, cost and durability against each other, names the effect on local workers, and reaches a reasoned view on balancing the two policies.
sampleAnswers.answer: Education and training funding and migration policy are two ways to close a skills shortage, and they differ in speed, cost and long-term effects. Funding for vocational education and training, delivered through TAFE institutes and registered training organisations, builds a durable local supply of electricians, carers and engineers. Its main strength is that workforce skills stay in the region and deepen over time, supporting long-term productivity. Its main weakness is time: an apprenticeship or diploma takes several years to complete, so vacancies may persist for much of that period. Training also carries a fiscal cost that the state budget must fund, and it does not guarantee that trainees will stay in the region once qualified. Migration policy is faster. Expanding skilled migration visas for the same occupations can fill vacancies within months, raising workforce size and the output the regional economy can produce. Migrants may bring specialised experience, and their spending creates demand for local goods and services. However, migration depends on federal visa settings and on migrants choosing to settle in the region. It can also ease wage pressure in the short run, which may leave local young people without a training pathway into the occupations that are most in demand. On balance, the trade-off is between immediacy and durability, and the time lags involved are the key difference. A region with an urgent shortage may need migration to meet immediate demand while training builds a local supply for the future. A region whose shortage is expected to persist should weight training more heavily, because it produces lasting gains in skills. The state should also weigh how each option fits its budget. A training program can be phased in over several years, whereas a visa increase depends on federal approval and on employers' capacity to recruit and house new workers. A sound response combines both: migration to fill urgent gaps, and funded training to build the pipeline that reduces reliance on migration over time.

sampleAnswers.feedback: A 5-mark response compares timing and cost but gives less weight to the effect on local workers and does not reach a clear view on balancing the policies.
sampleAnswers.answer: Training funding takes several years to produce qualified electricians and carers, so it does not solve a shortage quickly. It is also costly for the state budget. Migration can fill vacancies faster, because visas bring in workers who are already qualified, but it depends on federal visa settings. Migration may reduce pressure on wages, which can make it harder for local workers to gain higher pay, so both options have downsides. Using both policies together may be sensible.

sampleAnswers.feedback: A 2-mark response describes the two policies with limited discussion of their trade-offs.
sampleAnswers.answer: Training takes a long time and migration is quicker. Both cost money.

sampleAnswers.answer: The NAIRU is the level of unemployment at which there is no cyclical unemployment. In order to reduce this, policies should aim to target structural or frictional unemployment. By improving occupational or geographical mobility of workers through reforms such as increasing training programmes and relocation assistance, the structurally unemployed can access a wider range of employment opportunities, making it easier for them to secure jobs that are available. Labour market policies that connect potential employees and employers more efficiently will reduce frictional unemployment and the NAIRU.

dotPoints.description: Effectiveness of labour market policies in achieving Australia’s economic objectives

prompts.question: Assess the effectiveness of labour market policies in achieving Australia’s economic objectives.
markerNotes: Strong answers judge labour market policies against employment growth and equity, recognising that minimum wage rises can improve equity but may affect employment for some
Reward reference to evidence, such as employment growth following the training and skilled migration programs
commonStudentErrors: Assessing labour market policy without evidence
Treating the minimum wage's effects on employment as settled
prompts.markingCriteria:
7-8 marks: Makes a sustained, criteria-based assessment of the effectiveness of labour market policies in achieving Australia's economic objectives, weighing their effects on employment, productivity and equity, and reaching a reasoned judgement
5-6 marks: Assesses effectiveness against at least one objective with accurate evidence and suggests a conclusion, with some weighing of the evidence for other objectives
4 marks: Describes labour market policies and their objectives with some relevant detail and a limited assessment of effectiveness
2-3 marks: Identifies or describes a labour market policy or objective with limited detail
1 mark: Makes a basic or general statement about labour market policy

sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: the answer assesses effectiveness against each objective separately, uses specific evidence and mechanisms, weighs the policies against one another, and reaches a reasoned judgement.
sampleAnswers.answer: The effectiveness of labour market policies varies across Australia's economic objectives, so the judgement depends on which objective is used. The evidence for apprenticeship support is strongest for productivity growth. It funds people to gain recognised trade skills, which raises the productivity of the workers who complete training, and the skills remain in the economy for many years. Its effect on unemployment is more limited, because apprenticeships take several years to complete and many participants already have jobs. Public employment services are most relevant to unemployment, because they match job seekers with vacancies and help people prepare for work. Their effect depends on the job seeker's barriers, and for people with long periods out of work, matching alone is often insufficient, so their effect on long-term unemployment is modest. Skilled migration addresses shortages directly and can ease wage pressure in occupations where local supply is short, but it does little to raise the productivity of existing workers, and it may reduce the incentive for local training in the occupations concerned. For equity, these policies have a limited direct effect on income distribution, since they depend on participation and their benefits are shared unevenly across groups. Productivity gains from apprenticeship support depend on how well training matches employer needs, so the policy is most effective where it is linked to industries that face skills shortages. Equity outcomes are shaped by how employment services are delivered, and the results for long-term unemployed people depend heavily on the intensity of the support. For a sound judgement, the review must therefore separate the effect on each objective rather than treating the policies as a single program. Taken together, the policies are most effective for productivity and skill supply, moderately effective for employment, and weakest for income distribution, so the review should judge them as partial rather than complete solutions.

sampleAnswers.feedback: A 5-mark response assesses effectiveness against one objective with accurate reasoning and suggests a conclusion, but it does not assess the policies against the other objectives.
sampleAnswers.answer: Apprenticeship support can increase the number of skilled workers, which supports productivity growth. Because the skills stay in the economy for years, this policy is effective against that objective. Its effect on unemployment in the short term is smaller, so the policy is partly effective overall.

sampleAnswers.feedback: A 2-mark response identifies a policy without assessing its effectiveness.
sampleAnswers.answer: Apprenticeship support and public employment services are labour market policies.

prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A government review assesses whether public employment services, apprenticeship support and skilled migration have helped Australia meet three objectives: low unemployment, productivity growth and an equitable distribution of income. The review must judge each policy against each objective separately, because the evidence for each differs.

prompts.question: Analyse the likely effects of a hypothetical wage subsidy for employers who hire long-term unemployed workers on employment, wages and inflation.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A government introduces a wage subsidy that pays employers $5 for each hour worked by a long-term unemployed person they hire, for a period of two years. Employers in the economy report difficulty finding experienced workers, and the economy is operating close to its capacity.
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Analyses clearly the likely effects of the wage subsidy on employment, wages and inflation, tracing the chain of cause and effect for each and explaining the conditions under which the effects would be larger or smaller
5 marks: Analyses the effects on employment and wages with accurate chains of reasoning
4 marks: Analyses one effect with accurate reasoning and a clear link to the subsidy
3 marks: Describes the wage subsidy and one of its likely effects with some accuracy
2 marks: Identifies a likely effect of the subsidy
1 mark: Makes a general statement about wage subsidies
markerNotes: Reward chains of reasoning such as lower hiring costs increasing labour demand, which raises employment and may push up wages, rather than assertions that the subsidy 'helps the economy'
Credit recognition that inflation effects depend on spare capacity, and that some subsidised hiring would have happened anyway
commonStudentErrors: Stating that the subsidy will reduce inflation without a chain of reasoning
Assuming every subsidised hire is a new job, without considering that some hiring would have occurred without the subsidy
Analysing only the employment effect and ignoring wages and inflation

sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: the answer traces each effect from the lower cost of hiring, links wages and inflation to the economy's spare capacity, and notes that some subsidised hiring would have happened anyway.
sampleAnswers.answer: The wage subsidy would work as a labour market policy, through the cost of labour to employers. Because it reduces the effective cost of each hour worked, employers face a lower cost of hiring long-term unemployed workers, and the demand for labour rises at each wage level. The first effect is on employment: more long-term unemployed people move into jobs, which lowers the unemployment rate and raises the number of people in work. The second effect is on wages. Where firms already report difficulty finding experienced workers, the extra demand for labour pushes up the wages employers must offer to attract workers from other firms. The third effect is on inflation. Higher employment and wages raise household incomes and spending, and because the economy is close to capacity, firms can pass higher labour costs into their prices. The employment gain is also smaller than the number of subsidised jobs, because some subsidised hires would have happened anyway. The effect on inflation is therefore conditional. If the labour market has spare capacity, the extra employment reduces unemployment with little effect on prices, whereas near full capacity the same policy adds to wage and price pressure. Overall, the subsidy raises employment, with wage and inflation pressure that depends on spare capacity.

sampleAnswers.feedback: A 4-mark response analyses the employment and wage effects with reasoning but does not extend the analysis to inflation or the conditions that change the size of the effects.
sampleAnswers.answer: The subsidy lowers the cost of hiring, so employers will demand more labour. More long-term unemployed people will be employed, which reduces unemployment. Because firms are already short of experienced workers, the extra demand for labour may push wages up as firms compete for staff.

sampleAnswers.feedback: A 2-mark response identifies an effect of the subsidy without reasoning about how it occurs.
sampleAnswers.answer: The subsidy will increase employment for long-term unemployed people.

dotPoints.description: Limitations to the effectiveness of labour market policies, including policy lags and political considerations

prompts.question: Explain the limitations to the effectiveness of labour market policies, including policy lags and political considerations.
markerNotes: Reward the explanation that training and migration reforms take years to change the skills of the workforce
Political considerations, such as opposition to changes in wage-setting, show a realistic account of limits
commonStudentErrors: Describing limitations without linking them to effectiveness
Assuming that labour market policies have immediate effects
prompts.markingCriteria:
6 marks: Explains clearly the limitations to the effectiveness of labour market policies, including policy lags and political considerations, with precise examples of how each reduces effectiveness
5 marks: Explains both limitations with accurate examples and at least one further constraint, linking each to the reduced effect of the program on the affected workers
4 marks: Explains one limitation with accurate detail and a relevant example, showing how it reduces the effectiveness of the policy in practice
3 marks: Describes limitations of labour market policy with some accuracy, but gives limited explanation of how either policy lags or political considerations reduce effectiveness
2 marks: Identifies a limitation of labour market policy, such as policy lags or political considerations, without explaining how it reduces effectiveness
1 mark: Makes a general statement about policy limits

sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: the answer explains both the policy lags and the political considerations with precise examples of how each reduces the program's effectiveness, and adds a further constraint.
sampleAnswers.answer: Labour market policies face limitations that reduce their effectiveness, and the retraining program offers clear examples. The first limitation is policy lags. A recognition lag arises when the government takes time to see that automation is causing long-term unemployment in particular towns, and a decision lag arises while the program is designed and funded. An implementation lag follows, because training providers must set up courses and workers must enrol. The main delay is the impact lag: courses take about two years to complete before workers can apply for jobs. The second limitation is political considerations. A government may prefer programs it can announce before an election, so it may favour short courses with quick completion numbers over longer training that leads to stable jobs. It may also change the program or end it before the impact lag has passed, so the workers who need it most may not benefit. A further constraint is that retraining cannot create jobs where few exist, so the program's effect depends on local demand for the new skills. Each lag adds to the next, so results may take years to observe. Together, these limitations mean the program may improve employment in the long run but is unlikely to show clear results within a single term of government.

sampleAnswers.feedback: A 3-mark response describes the limitations with some accuracy but gives only a brief example and does not explain how the political considerations affect the program.
sampleAnswers.answer: The retraining courses take about two years, so the program's effect on unemployment is delayed. Governments may also change the program before the results are seen.

sampleAnswers.feedback: A 1-mark response makes a general statement about policy limits without identifying a specific limitation.
sampleAnswers.answer: Labour market programs do not always work well.

prompts.question: Account for the policy lags and political considerations that may reduce the effectiveness of a hypothetical apprenticeship subsidy.
prompts.scenario: Hypothetical: A state government announces a subsidy for employers who hire new apprentices in the building trades. It expects the subsidy to reduce a shortage of trades workers within two years. The subsidy will be introduced in the next state budget and reviewed before the next state election.

markerNotes: Reward the link between each lag and the outcome, such as an implementation lag delaying new apprentices entering training

sampleAnswers.feedback: Full marks: the answer separates the recognition, decision, implementation and impact lags, explains how the electoral cycle shortens the time for results, and links each point to the outcome.
sampleAnswers.answer: The apprenticeship subsidy is limited by policy lags. A recognition lag occurs before the government identifies the shortage, and a decision lag occurs while the subsidy is designed and approved in the budget. An implementation lag follows, as training providers and employers adjust before apprentices are hired, and an impact lag means apprentices take several years to finish. The shortage may persist for much of that period. Political considerations also limit effectiveness. The electoral cycle is usually shorter than the time apprentices need to finish their qualifications, so the government is judged on outcomes it cannot yet deliver. Before an election, the government may review or cut the subsidy before the impact lag has ended.

sampleAnswers.answer: A policy lag means the subsidy takes time to work, because apprentices need years to finish training.

sampleAnswers.answer: Politicians may not always make the best decisions.

sampleAnswers.answer: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander land and water management practices inform environmental policy. Caring for Country treats land, water and cultural values as one responsibility, so managers plan work across the whole landscape. Cultural burning reduces the build-up of fuel, which lowers the risk and cost of severe fires and the public spending on emergency response. Water monitoring by Traditional Owners gives agencies information about river and wetland health that supports decisions on water allocation and pollution control. Formal roles for these managers, such as ranger programs, also create local jobs and skills that connect environmental management to the local economy.

sampleAnswers.answer: Command-and-control instruments set direct rules that firms must follow, rather than relying on price signals. Bans prohibit a product or activity outright, such as the cleaning chemical banned from use in the plants. Restrictions limit an activity without banning it, such as a cap on the volume of wastewater each plant may discharge. Efficiency standards set a minimum performance level that a plant must meet whatever its costs. Technical specifications require a particular method or equipment, such as the filtration system that every plant must install. The regulator can then check compliance through inspections and penalties.
